law:
Trade Secrets Enterprise Guide issued by Intellectual Property Office of Singapore;

Common Law doctrine of breach of confidence
impact:
In Singapore, there is no express legislation for the protection of trade secrets per se. Instead, protection of trade secrets in Singapore is typically through the common law doctrine of breach of confidence, as well as (where applicable) the use of IP and contract law. It protects all types of confidential information, such as your personal/private information (e.g., medical reports, photographs, receipts).

For information to be protectable as confidential information or a trade secret, it must not already be available to the public at large and it must be clearly and specifically identified (Nanofilm Technologies International Pte Ltd v Semivac International Pte Ltd and others [2018] SGHC 167). 

Additionally, the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore's Trade Secrets Enterprise Guide reports: In considering whether a breach of confidence is made out, the following will be considered: 1) whether the information has the quality of confidentiality; 2) whether the information was imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidentiality. An obligation of confidentiality can be found even where confidential information has been accessed or acquired without the company’s knowledge or consent; 3) whether the person who came into the information is able to demonstrate that his conscience was unaffected.  For instance that he was not aware that the information was confidential or he came across the information by accident.

Confidential information is protected by the common law doctrine – law of confidence, as well as contract law and various legislation(s) dependent on the circumstance. 

• For example, section 3 of the Computer Misuse Act 1993 may apply in cases where a person breaches cybersecurity in order to gain access to trade secrets whilst section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act obligates the organisation collecting personal data to protect the personal data by making reasonable security arrangements. 
The Trade Secrets Enterprise Guide issued by the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore provides further guidance on this.
note:
"Trade secrets are generally regarded at common law as a form of confidential information that has a higher degree of confidentiality than “mere confidential information” (see, for example, Clearlab SG Pte Ltd v Ting Chong Chai [2014] SGHC 221 at [68]). For information to be protectable as confidential information or a trade secret, it must not already be available to the public at large and it must be clearly and specifically identified (Nanofilm Technologies International Pte Ltd v Semivac International Pte Ltd and others [2018] SGHC 167). Information is more likely to be considered confidential where: The release of the information would injure the owner of the information or benefit others; The owner believes the information to be secret and not already in the public domain and the owner’s belief is reasonable; and The information is considered confidential when judged in the light of usage and practices of the particular trade or industry concerned. https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-trade-secrets/singapore "

impact:
According to Section 26, an organisation may only transfer personal data outside Singapore if it has taken appropriate steps to ensure that: 
- it will comply with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) obligations in respect of the transferred personal data while it remains in its possession or under its control; and 
- the recipient outside of Singapore is bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide a standard of protection to the personal data transferred that is comparable to that under the PDPA. 

In this regard, “legally enforceable obligations” would include obligations imposed on the recipient: (i) under law (e.g. the recipient’s relevant national data privacy legislation); (ii) under any contract: (a) requiring the recipient to provide a standard of protection to the personal data transferred that is at least comparable to the protection under the PDPA; and (b) specifying the countries and territories to which the personal data may be transferred under the contract; (iii) under binding corporate rules (see below); or (iv) any other legally binding instrument.

law:
Personal Data Protection Act 2012;

Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2020
impact:
The Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (PDPA) provides a baseline standard of protection for personal data in Singapore. It complements sector-specific legislative and regulatory frameworks such as the Banking Act and Insurance Act, Healthcare Services Act, Telecommunications Act, etc. The PDPA comprises various requirements governing the collection, use, disclosure and care of personal data in Singapore. Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) administers and enforces the PDPA.

Moreover, the PDPA amendment in 2021 introduces a number of key reforms, including mandatory data breach notification requirements, amendments to the consent obligation, offences for egregious mishandling of personal data, prohibitions relating to the use of dictionary attacks and address-harvesting software, and the PDPC's power to accept voluntary undertakings as part of its enforcement regime.
timeframe:
Since 2012 last amended on 1 February 2021;

Since February 2021
note:
"The PDPA does not expressly include cookies in its definition of personal data. However, cookies can qualify as personal data if they fall within the broad definition of personal data, that is, if they identify an individual either by themselves or together with other information, which the organisation has or is likely to have access to. Likewise, digital fingerprinting and online behavioural advertising technologies will fall under the ambit of the PDPA insofar as they deal with personal data. The PDPC of Singapore has issued guidance that expressly discusses cookies as a way in which personal data is collected, used or disclosed. In essence, the Commission recognises that many internet activities today are dependent on the use of cookies and that unnecessarily restricting the use of cookies will impede the use of the internet. However, because cookies can potentially collect personal data, organisations must be mindful of using them for individuals' online activities. If cookies containing personal data arise from individuals who voluntarily provide it, their consent can be deemed to be provided for the purpose for which the personal data was provided. However, the obligation to obtain an individual's consent to collect personal data rests with the organisation that is collecting it, whether itself or through data intermediaries. Where an organisation operates a website that a third party uses to collect personal data, and the website operator itself is not collecting this personal data, the obligation is on the third party organisation to obtain the required consent."

law: Cybersecurity Act 2018
impact: Cybersecurity Act 2018 establishes a legal framework for the oversight and maintenance of national cybersecurity in Singapore. The key objectives of the Cybersecurity Act are to: (i) strengthen the protection of Critical Information Infrastructure against cyber-attacks; (ii) authorize the government to prevent and respond to cybersecurity threats and incidents; (iii); establish a framework for sharing cybersecurity information, and (iv) establish a licensing framework for cybersecurity service providers. Amendments to the Act were made in May 2024 to update the Act so that it keeps pace with the developments in the cyber threat landscape, as well as our evolving technological operating context. The key amendments: (i) updated existing provisions relating to cybersecurity of Critical Information Infrastructure, and (ii) expanded CSA’s oversight to cover new classes of regulated entities.
note: ‘Cybersecurity Act 2018 mandates the identification and designation of CIIs—computer systems essential for delivering vital services. Owners of CIIs are required to implement robust cybersecurity measures and comply with codes of practice to prevent and respond to cyber threats. CII owners must promptly report cybersecurity incidents to the Commissioner of Cybersecurity. The Act grants the Commissioner authority to investigate and manage such incidents to mitigate potential impacts. Cybersecurity Act 2018 introduces a licensing framework for providers of specific cybersecurity services, ensuring that these services meet established standards and are delivered by qualified professionals. It also formalizes the CSA's role as the national authority overseeing cybersecurity, responsible for implementing policies, coordinating responses to cyber incidents, and promoting cybersecurity awareness.’ This write-up has been re-written by Singapore feedback.

law: Copyright Act 2021
impact:
The Part 6 Division 2 of Copyright Act 2021 creates a “safe-harbour + notice-and-takedown” regime for network service providers (NSPs) and network connection providers (NCPs) in Singapore. The purposes are to Shield providers from monetary liability (damages, profits, statutory damages) when their networks are used for copyright infringement, provided they meet the statutory conditions, and
limit available court remedies to narrowly defined, non-monetary orders—mainly disabling access, removing or restoring content, or terminating specific accounts.

Four protected technical activities include Transmission, routing or providing connections (§316), System caching (§317), Storage at a user’s direction (§318), Referring or linking via search engines, hyperlinks, etc. (§319)
For each activity, the statute lists precise conditions (automatic processes, no editorial control, no direct financial benefit from infringement, expeditious compliance with takedown notices, designation of a notice agent, etc.).

Providers who act in good faith to remove or disable access are immunised from liability, even if the content is later found non-infringing.
Affected users may file a “restoration notice”; the provider must restore the material unless the rights owner commences court action within 10 working days.
There is no obligation to monitor networks proactively.
Safe-harbour eligibility is rebuttably presumed if prescribed evidence is produced.
Making a false statement in any notice is an offence (up to S$10,000 or 2 years’ imprisonment) and exposes the sender to damages.
Overall, the Division codifies a balanced framework: providers that play a passive, technical role obtain strong liability protection, while rights owners retain a quick, low-cost mechanism to address apparent infringements.
note:
The Safe Harbour provisions are encapsulated within ss 193B to 193D and ss 252A to 252C of the Copyright Act. A network service provider (NSP) elects not to meet the requirements does not automatically make it liable to copyright holders for any copyright infringements.

Owners and exclusive licensees of copyright can apply to the High Court of Singapore for an order requiring an ISP to take reasonable steps to disable access to a "flagrantly infringing online location" (FIOL). FIOLs are defined in the Copyright Act as online locations that have been or are being used to flagrantly commit or facilitate rights infringements.

Relevant orders that can be granted include site-blocking orders, as well as "dynamic" injunctions that require the ISPs to block new domain names, URLs and/or IP addresses that provide access to essentially the same websites. Both were granted by the Singapore High Court in Disney Enterprises, Inc and others v M1 Limited and others, where Disney and five other major film studios applied for site-block orders against the five main retail ISPs in Singapore.' This content summarizes Singapore’s existing site-blocking regime under the Copyright Act: how rights owners can get court orders to block “flagrantly infringing online locations,” and that failure to satisfy the Safe-Harbour conditions does not automatically expose a provider to liability. 
While Division 2 of the Act States the detailed statutory “safe-harbour” provisions, which spell out exactly when and how network service providers are shielded from monetary remedies and what limited non-monetary orders may still be granted, together with the notice-and-takedown procedures.

In 1999, Singapore made its first amendments to the Copyright Act to introduce various safe harbor defenses for Internet intermediaries as network service providers. Arising from its obligations under the US- Singapore Free Trade Agreement, Singapore further revised in 2014 the safe harbor defenses in the Copyright Act for network service providers.

note: "The key areas of liability for website content are: - If the website does not comply with certain regulatory requirements (for example, personal data requirements under the PDPA), a regulatory authority can require the website operator to comply with the applicable provisions. The authority can also impose fines and imprisonment if the requirements are breached. - If the website operator uses third party content online without obtaining the relevant rights, it may be exposed to claims of IP infringement. There are various IP-specific statutes in Singapore, which set out the scope of rights for intellectual property rights owners. - Under the common law and the Defamation Act 1957 (2020 Rev Ed), where content published on a website is defamatory, the victim can obtain damages and/or an injunction requiring removal of the offending content from the website. - Under the Protection from Harassment Act (2020 Rev Ed), there are penalties against behaviour that causes or which is likely to cause harassment, alarm and distress to victims. Directions can also be issued by the Minister to correct or stop the communication of the falsehood. - Under the Undesirable Publications Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed), there are statutory offences that could potentially be committed through the online publication of obscene material. The penalty for publishing obscene material can result in both imprisonment and a fine. - Under the Spam Control Act 2007 (2020 Rev Ed), there are penalties for online businesses that engage in unsolicited commercial communications through their website."

law: Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act 2019
impact: In both intent and practice, the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) relies primarily on Correction Directions to dispel falsehoods. Correction Directions require facts to be juxtaposed against falsehoods, which are not subject to removal or restricted access. Members of the public can read both the facts and the falsehoods and make up their own minds. Access blocking measures under POFMA are only intended to be used against the most egregious of cases (e.g. malicious deepfakes). As of 31 May 2025, no Disabling Direction under POFMA has been issued. Section 28(4) of POFMA does not impose liability on internet intermediaries. Rather, it provides a safe harbour for internet access service providers in relation to access blocking orders. The safe harbour provisions for internet intermediaries should also include Sections 15(3), 16(4), 27(4), 33(5), 34(6), 39(2), 42(3), 43(4), 51(2) and 54(5) of POFMA.

The SCAP is issued by the Advertising Standards Authority of Singapore (ASAS), an advisory council under the Consumers Association of Singapore and was drafted against the background of international law and practice, including the International Code of Advertising Practice issued by the International Chamber of Commerce. The purpose of the SCAP is to promote a high standard of ethics in advertising by self-regulation. As such, the ASAS relies principally on a system of guidance and voluntary compliance, rather than punitive measures, to facilitate observance of the SCAP. Although the SCAP does not have the force of law, it has been endorsed by organisations representing advertisers, advertising agencies and the media. The SCAP includes general guidelines that all advertisements must comply with, as well as certain industry-specific guidelines. Generally, under the SCAP, all advertisements (regardless of industry and mode of advertisement), must meet the following requirements: Be truthful. Not incite people to engage in illegal activities. Not be offensive to prevailing norms of decency. Not undermine social and family values. The SCAP includes specific guidelines for advertising and marketing communication that appear on social media (see Guidelines on Interactive Marketing Communication and Social Media), which impose disclosure requirements for certain types of sponsorship arrangements and commercial relationships."

note: "MAS has released the ""E-Payments User Protection Guidelines"" which provide general guidance and should be read in conjunction with the relevant legislation and subsidiary legislation, codes, and notices. The aim of this guideline is to protect users of electronic payments from security threats and fraud and to provide more security to electronic payment transactions for individuals and micro-enterprises. For example, users who use e-payment systems must provide accurate contact information and protect their passwords, while businesses using e-payment must monitor transactions and cultivate good security measures. The Payment Services Act was passed in 2019 to regulate the provision of payment services. "Payment services" are defined in the First Schedule of the Act to include account issuance services, domestic money transfer services, and e-money issuance services. Under the Act, providers of payment services must hold a licence and comply with requirements calibrated according to the risks that specific payment services and business models pose. The Payment Services (Amendment) Bill was passed in 2021 The Payment Services (Amendment) Regulations was passed in 2024 to regulate digital payment token service providers. The aim of these amendments was to deal with the anti-money laundering and countering terrorist financing risks that are often associated with cryptocurrencies. Key amendments include the imposition of additional requirements in respect of licensees providing digital payment token services, as well as expanding the general duty to use reasonable care not to provide false information to both individuals as well as corporate entities."

Article 1 of the Circular sets the scope of merger and acquisition security reviews, including: (1) Foreign investors acquiring domestic military enterprises and enterprises supporting military industries, enterprises located near key and sensitive military facilities, as well as other entities related to national defense security; and (2) Foreign investors acquiring domestic enterprises involved in key areas related to national security, such as important agricultural products, critical energy and resources, vital infrastructure, essential transportation services, core technologies, and major equipment manufacturing, where the actual control of the enterprise may be obtained by foreign investors.

Article 2 states the content of merger and acquisition security reviews:
1. The impact of the merger or acquisition transaction on national defense security, including its effect on the domestic production capacity of products needed for national defense, the ability to provide domestic services, and related equipment and facilities.
2. The impact of the merger or acquisition transaction on the stable operation of the national economy.
3. The impact of the merger or acquisition transaction on the basic social living order.
4. The impact of the merger or acquisition transaction on the research and development capabilities of critical technologies related to national security.

law: Measures for Security Review of Foreign Investments 《外商投资安全审查办法》
impact:
According to Article 2 of the Measure for Security Review of Foreign Investments, the types of transactions carried out by foreign investors directly or indirectly in China that may be subject to security review include the following: (i) investments by foreign investors by themselves or jointly with other investors, that are investing in any new project or establishing a business in China; (ii) foreign investors that are acquiring equity or assets of domestic business through mergers and acquisitions; and (iii) foreign investors making investments into China through other methods.

Article 4 states that Foreign investments in the important information technology and Internet products and services, major equipment, key technologies sectors must be declared to the office of the Operational Mechanism (the office is set up under the Measure for the review of foreign investments), to the extent that the investment has a bearing on national security and the that actual control of the investee enterprise is required. Actual control has been been said to exist when the total amount of foreign investment is larger than 50% or the foreign investor is able to affect the board, shareholder meetings or the essential personnel who decide the operation, human resources, finance or key technology of the company.

Pursuant to review, the Operational Mechanism can decide that the foreign investment will not affect national security, in which case the security review has been passed. If it is decided that the foreign investment will affect national security, the parties to the investment may be required to accept the attached conditions which will govern the investment. If the Operational Mechanism decides to prohibit the investment, the same shall not be carried out.

law: Ministry of Commerce Order No. 4 of 2020 on the List of Unreliable Entities 《商务部2020年第4号令 不可靠实体名单规定》
impact:
The Ministry of Commerce Order No. 4 of 2020 on the List of Unreliable Entities sets up a list of unreliable enterprises. As per the Order, foreign entities classified as unreliable entities could face sanctions in the form of restrictions or prohibition on the foreign entity from engaging in China-related import or export activities, restrictions on prohibition on the foreign entity from investing in China etc. Foreign entities that could be included in the unreliable entity list include those involved in international commerce or related activities that engage in endangering national sovereignty, security or development interests in China, suspending normal transactions against any organization or individual in China, entities which violate market principles and cause damage to the rights and interests of the Chinese entity. Under this Order, a special unit in MOFCOM will be responsible for identifying foreign entities (which include foreign enterprises, organizations and individuals) that will be subject to restrictions. 

In February 2023, the Unreliable Entities List Working Mechanism headed by China’s Ministry of Commerce has for the first time designated two US aerospace and defense companies as “Unreliable Entities”. So far, no firms in digital trade related sectors have been designated as an unreliable entity.

law: Patent Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国专利法》
impact:
Civil and administrative procedures:
Articles 46 and 63 allow parties to appeal administrative decisions related to invalidity and compulsory licensing by filing lawsuits with the courts.
Article 46: Any organization or individual who believes that the grant of a patent does not comply with the provisions of this Law may request the administrative department for patent affairs under the State Council to declare the patent right invalid. The administrative department for patent affairs under the State Council shall promptly examine and decide on the request for invalidation of the patent right and notify the parties concerned. The decision on the invalidation of a patent right shall be registered and announced by the administrative department for patent affairs under the State Council. The decision shall be final and binding.
Article 63: In the event of a dispute over patent infringement, the parties concerned may resolve the dispute through mediation. If mediation fails, or if one of the parties refuses mediation, they may bring a lawsuit to the people's court or request the relevant administrative department for patents to handle the matter.
When the relevant administrative department for patents determines the matter, if a party is dissatisfied with the handling decision, they may bring a lawsuit to the people's court within 15 days from the date of receiving the notification. If no lawsuit is brought within the prescribed time limit, the decision shall come into effect and be enforced by the people's court.

Remedies:
Article 71: When the amount of damages for patent infringement cannot be determined based on the losses suffered by the patent holder, the benefits obtained by the infringer, or a reasonable multiple of the patent license fee, the People's Court may award damages ranging from RMB 30,000 to RMB 5,000,000, depending on factors such as the type of patent, nature, and circumstances of the infringement. Where intentional infringement occurs under severe circumstances, the People's Court may determine compensation up to five times the amount calculated based on the above methods. The amount of damages shall also include the reasonable expenses incurred by the patent holder in stopping the infringement.

Provisional Measures:
Article 69 provides patent enforcement agencies the authority to inspect, seize, and secure evidence during suspected patent infringement or counterfeiting investigations.
timeframe: Since April 1984, last amended in June 2021

law: Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国著作权法》
impact:
Civil and administrative measures:
Article 49. To protect copyright and rights related to copyright, rights holders may adopt technical measures.
Without the permission of the rights holder, no organization or individual may intentionally circumvent or disable such technical measures, manufacture, import, or provide to the public devices or components intended for the purpose of circumventing or disabling technical measures, or intentionally provide technical services to others for the same purpose. Exceptions apply in circumstances where circumvention is permitted by law or administrative regulations.
The "technical measures" referred to in this law are effective technologies, devices, or components used to prevent or restrict the unauthorized browsing, viewing, or enjoyment of works, performances, or audio-visual recordings, or their provision to the public through information networks.

Remedies:
Article 52 states that those commit infringement shall, depending on the circumstances, bear civil liabilities such as ceasing the infringement, eliminating the impact, making a formal apology, and compensating for losses.
Furthermore, Article 53 states that If the infringement also harms the public interest, the copyright administration department shall order the cessation of the infringing act, issue a warning, confiscate any illegal gains, and seize or harmlessly destroy the infringing copies, as well as the materials, tools, and equipment primarily used to produce such copies. If the illegal business revenue exceeds 50,000 yuan, a fine of one to five times the revenue may also be imposed. If there is no illegal business revenue, or the revenue is difficult to calculate or less than 50,000 yuan, a fine of up to 250,000 yuan may be imposed. If the act constitutes a crime, criminal liability shall be pursued in accordance with the law.

Provisional measures:
Article 56
If a copyright owner or a holder of rights related to copyright has evidence proving that another party is infringing or is about to infringe upon their rights, thereby obstructing the realization of their rights, and if failure to stop such actions in time may cause irreparable harm to their legitimate interests, they may apply to the People's Court for measures such as property preservation, orders to perform specific actions, or orders to prohibit specific actions before filing a lawsuit, in accordance with the law.
Article 57
To prevent infringement, in cases where evidence may be destroyed or difficult to obtain later, the copyright owner or a holder of rights related to copyright may apply to the People's Court for evidence preservation before filing a lawsuit, in accordance with the law.
timeframe: Since September 1990, last amended in June 2021

Interim Administrative Measures for Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into effect on August 15, 2023.
Security assessment and filing: Although the Generative AI Measures do not explicitly identify high-risk services, generative AI services associated with public opinion or social mobilization attributes must undergo security assessment and algorithm filing (Article 17). Regulators may target information services enabling public expression and participation in activities, like Internet forums, blogs, chat rooms, public accounts, short videos, and webcasts, in line with other Chinese regulations. To fulfill the filling procedure, provider's name, service form, application field, algorithm type, algorithm self-assessment report, intended public disclosure content are required to be recorded. Thus, no mandatory disclosure of trade secrets is involved in the algorithm filling process.

impact:
China has not legislated a unified law specifically directed to trade secret protection. So far in China, the laws related to trade secret protection scatter across the Anti-Unfair Competition Law (revised in 2019), the Civil Code (effective in 2021), the Labour Law (revised in 2018), and the Criminal Law (revised in 2020).

According to the Anti-Unfair Competition Law: trade secrets refer to any technical information, operational information or commercial information, which is not known to the public and has commercial value, and for which its infringer adopted measures to ensure its confidentiality (Article 9). 

Article 21 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law further states that where a business operator or any other natural person, legal person or unincorporated organisation infringes any trade secret in violation of Article 9 herein, the supervision and inspection authority shall order it to cease the illegal act, confiscated the illegal gains and impose on it a fine of between CNY100, 000 and CNY1 million; where the circumstance is serious, the fine shall be between CNY500, 000 and CNY5 million.

Furthermore, Article 219 of the Criminal Law writes:
Anyone who commits any of the following acts of infringing on trade secrets, and if the circumstances are serious, shall be sentenced to imprisonment of not more than three years, along with a fine or a standalone fine; if the circumstances are particularly serious, they shall be sentenced to imprisonment of more than three years but not more than ten years, and fined:

- Obtaining a trade secret of the rights holder through theft, bribery, fraud, coercion, electronic intrusion, or other improper means;

- Disclosing, using, or allowing others to use the trade secret of the rights holder obtained through the means described in the previous item;

- Disclosing, using, or allowing others to use a trade secret in their possession in violation of confidentiality obligations or the requirements of the rights holder regarding the confidentiality of the trade secret.

Any person who, knowing the acts listed in the preceding paragraph, obtains, discloses, uses, or allows others to use the trade secret shall be deemed to have infringed on trade secrets.
note:
The United States-China Economic and Trade Agreement (Phase One Agreement), signed in January 2020, includes several trade secret commitments to address a number of long-standing concerns in China, including on expanding the scope of civil liability, covering acts such as electronic intrusions as trade secret theft, shifting the burden of producing evidence, making it easier to obtain preliminary injunctions to prevent use of stolen trade secrets, allowing criminal investigations without need to show actual losses, ensuring criminal enforcement for willful misappropriation, and prohibiting unauthorized disclosure of trade secrets and confidential business information by government personnel or third-party experts.

Source: https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/IssueAreas/IP/2022%20Special%20301%20Report.pdf

impact:

Article 17
Telecommunication networks shall achieve interconnection and intercommunication in accordance with the principles of technical feasibility, economic rationality, fairness, impartiality, and mutual cooperation.

A dominant telecommunication service provider shall not refuse interconnection and intercommunication requests made by other telecommunication service providers or dedicated network operators.

The "dominant telecommunication service provider" mentioned in the preceding paragraph refers to an operator that controls essential telecommunication infrastructure, holds a significant market share in the telecommunication services market, and can substantially affect the ability of other operators to enter the market.

law: Administrative Measures for the Licensing of Telecommunication Business 《电信业务经营许可管理办法》
impact:
In China, telecommunication services can be categorized into two groups: basic telecom services and value-added telecom services.

- Basic telecom services refer to services that provide public network infrastructure, public data transmission, and basic voice communication services.
- Value-added telecom services refer to services that utilize public network infrastructure to provide telecom and information services.

According to Article 5 of the Administrative Measures, to operate basic telecom services, the following conditions must be met: (1) the operator must be a company legally established specifically for engaging in basic telecom services, with no less than 51% of state-owned equity or shares; (2) there must be a business development research report and a network construction technical plan; (3) there must be sufficient funds and professional personnel suitable for the business activities; (4) there must be premises, facilities, and corresponding resources for conducting business activities; (5) there must be a reputation or capability to provide long-term services to users; (6) for operations within a province, autonomous region, or municipality, the minimum registered capital must be 100 million RMB, while for nationwide or cross-provincial operations, the minimum registered capital must be 1 billion RMB; (7) the company and its major investors and senior management personnel must not be listed on the telecom business dishonesty list; and (8) other conditions stipulated by the state.

Furthermore, Article 6 states that to operate value-added telecom services, the following conditions must be met: (1) the operator must be a company legally established; (2) possess sufficient funds and professional personnel suitable for conducting business activities; (3) have the credibility or capability to provide long-term services to users; (4) for operations within a province, autonomous region, or municipality, the minimum registered capital requirement is 1 million RMB, while for nationwide or cross-provincial operations, the minimum registered capital requirement is 10 million RMB; (5) have necessary premises, facilities, and technical solutions; (6) the company and its major investors and senior management personnel must not be listed on the telecom business dishonesty list; and (7) meet other conditions stipulated by the state.

law: Provisions on Promoting and Regulating Cross-border Data Flow《促进和规范数据跨境流动规定》
impact:
The Provisions clarify the applicable standards for data processors in cross-border data transfers, including security assessment, standard contract for outbound transfer of personal data, and personal information protection certification. Critical information infrastructure operators (CIIOs) shall undergo a security assessment when transferring personal information or important data outside China.  Other entities also need to conduct a security assessment when transferring important data or a large volume of personal information, with specific thresholds set at personal information (without sensitive personal information) of more than 1 million individuals or sensitive personal information of more than 10,000 individuals accumulated from January 1 of the current year.

Furthermore, the Provisions includes specific scenario exemptions: 

Article 2: Data processors shall identify and report important data in accordance with relevant regulations. If the relevant authorities or regions have not notified or publicly designated the data as important data, data processors are not required to declare it as important data for a data export security assessment.

Article 3: Data generated from international activities (e.g., trade, transportation, academic cooperation, manufacturing, marketing) that does not include personal or important data is exempt from cross-border data security assessments and compliance requirements.

Article 4: Personal information collected abroad and processed in China before being transferred overseas, as long as no domestic personal or important data is involved, is exempt from cross-border data security assessments and compliance requirements.

Article 5: Certain cross-border personal information transfers are exempt from security assessments and compliance requirements, including (1) fulfilling contracts (e.g., cross-border shopping, visa processing), (2) managing international human resources, (3) handling emergencies, and (4) transferring personal data abroad under a 100,000-person threshold (excluding sensitive data). Personal information provided abroad must not include important data.

law: Data Security Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国数据安全法》
impact: On June 10, 2021, the Data Security Law of the People’s Republic of China was officially passed during the 29th session of the Standing Committee of the 13th National People’s Congress. Aiming to further strengthen the current protection regime for the country’s fast-growing digital economy, the law stipulates how data is used, collected, developed, and protected in China. It emphasizes on top-down coordination of data security implementation among local governments and differentiated fines based on severity of violations.

In addition to comprehensive legislation that applies horizontally across all sectors, China has also developed and implemented a wide range of sector-specific regulations related to data protection, offering detailed guidance tailored to different industries. For example, in just the first half of 2024 alone, the Chinese government issued over 20 national laws, industry regulations, and local policies concerning data security. A selection of these is listed below.

Education sector: 
The General Office of the Ministry of Education Issued the “Management Standards for the Entry and Removal of Digital Educational Resources on the National Smart Education Platform”. According to the Standards, platform service providers must comply with relevant laws, regulations, and national standards, and adopt technical and other necessary measures to ensure the security of the platform and its resources, as well as retain network logs in accordance with the law.

Healthcare sector: 
The National Health Commission, the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine, and the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration jointly issued the "Notice on Further Advancing the Electronic Information Management of Physicians". The Notice calls on local authorities to implement a data security accountability system, strengthen data security monitoring and early warning mechanisms, regularly conduct security assessments and risk evaluations, and establish disaster recovery and data backup systems to ensure the security of information within electronic registration systems.

Finance sector: 
The Ministry of Finance and the Cyberspace Administration of China jointly issued the "Interim Measures for Data Security Management of Accounting Firms". The Measures require accounting firms to classify and categorize data in accordance with relevant laws, regulations, and the data classification standards applicable to the industry of the audited entity. Firms must identify core data, important data, and general data, and comply with specific requirements regarding the storage, transmission, and logging of core and important data.

Energy sector: 
The Ministry of Ecology and Environment, together with 14 other departments, jointly issued the "Implementation Plan for Establishing a Carbon Footprint Management System". The Plan calls for strengthening the protection of data security and intellectual property related to product carbon footprints. It emphasizes the implementation of data security laws and regulations, enhanced oversight of data circulation, and the creation of a secure and reliable environment for data exchange. The Plan also encourages digital technology enterprises to provide cloud-based security services to improve overall data security standards.

The Cybersecurity Law, which came into force on 1 June 2017, is the law covering various aspects of network security and has laid the foundation for a comprehensive cybersecurity regulatory regime in China. So far, a series of specific measures aimed at facilitating the implementation of the Cybersecurity Law have already been enacted, such as the Measures for Cybersecurity Review and the National Emergency Response Plan for Cybersecurity Incidents.

Article 15 stipulates that internet information service providers shall not produce, copy, publish, or disseminate information containing the following content:
1. Opposing the basic principles as they are confirmed in the Constitution.
2. Jeopardizing the security of the nation, divulging state secrets, subverting state power, or jeopardizing the integrity of the nation's unity
3. Harming the honor or the interests of the nation
4. Inciting hatred against peoples, racism against peoples, or disrupting the solidarity of peoples
5. Disrupting national policies on religion, propagating evil cults and feudal superstitions
6. Spreading rumors, disturbing social order or disrupting social stability
7. Spreading obscenity, pornography, gambling, violence, murder, terror, or abetting the commission of a crime
8. Insulting or defaming third parties, infringing on the legal rights and interests of third parties
9. Containing any other content prohibited by law or administrative rules

Furthermore, Article 20: Producing, copying, publishing, or disseminating any of the content listed in Article 15 of these Measures that constitutes a crime shall be subject to criminal liability in accordance with the law. For commercial internet information service providers, the licensing authority shall order them to suspend operations for rectification or revoke their business license and notify the enterprise registration authority. For non-commercial internet information service providers, the filing authority shall order the temporary closure of the website, up to and including permanent shutdown.

Thus, this Regulation provides legal basis for blocking and filtering commercial web content.

law: Commercial Web Content Blocking and Filtering in Practice
impact:
According to Freedom on the Net 2024 Country Report, the government maintains control over China’s gateways to the global internet, giving authorities the ability to restrict connectivity or access to content hosted on servers outside the country. This arrangement is the foundation for the “Great Firewall,” the informal name for the government’s comprehensive internet censorship system. All service providers must subscribe via the gateway operators, which are overseen by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT).

According to GreatFire.org—an anticensorship group that tracks filtering in China—as of February 2024, over 100,000 websites were blocked in China. Many international news outlets and their Chinese-language websites are blocked, such as those of the New York Times, Reuters, the Wall Street Journal, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), and the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).

Most international social media and messaging platforms are blocked, including Facebook, WhatsApp, Twitter, Instagram, Signal, Clubhouse, YouTube, Telegram, Snapchat, Line, and Pinterest. The popular discussion forum Reddit was blocked in August 2018, while all languages of Wikipedia were blocked in April 2019. A number of Google services—including Maps, Translate, Calendar, Docs, Drive, Scholar, and Analytics—remained blocked as of the end of the coverage period.

Blocks on global search engines severely limit the content available on the Chinese internet. Google’s search engine has been blocked since 2012, while the Yahoo search function was blocked in 2018.

A minority of Chinese internet users, though they number in the tens of millions, access blocked websites with circumvention tools like VPNs. However, the government has intensified its restrictions on these tools since 2017, when the MIIT banned the use of unlicensed VPNs.

Under the regulation, Internet information services are classified into two categories: commercial and non-commercial.

- Commercial internet information services refer to activities that provide information, webpage creation, or other services to internet users for a fee.
- Non-commercial internet information services refer to activities that provide open and shared information to internet users free of charge.

According to Article 7, entities engaging in commercial internet information services must apply for an Internet Information Service Value-Added Telecommunications Business License (hereinafter referred to as the Operating License) from the telecommunications regulatory authority of the province, autonomous region, municipality, or the competent department of the State Council responsible for the information industry.

The relevant telecommunications regulatory authority shall review the application and make a decision within 60 days of receiving it. If approved, an Operating License shall be issued. If denied, the applicant shall be notified in writing with an explanation of the reasons.

After obtaining the Operating License, the applicant must use it to complete the business registration process with the relevant enterprise registration authority.

law: Catalogue for the Administration of Import and Export Licenses for Dual-Use Items and Technologies《两用物项和技术进出口许可证管理目录》
impact:
According to the 2025 Catalogue for the Administration of Import and Export Licenses for Dual-Use Items and Technologies, the following ICT goods require an export license: 

high-performance digital computers, integrated circuit chips (security chips), encryption devices, encryption cards, encrypted VPN devices, cryptographic analysis equipment, electronic devices and components, scanning cameras, framing cameras with a recording rate exceeding 225,000 frames per second, framing cameras with a frame exposure time of ≤50 ns, and radiation-resistant television cameras and their lenses.

Notably, the names of the goods listed are based on the reference product names provided in the Catalogue for the Administration of Import and Export Licenses for Dual-Use Items and Technologies. However, the original catalogue provides more detailed descriptions of the specific types of items that require an export license.

For example, "high-performance digital computers" is quoted based on the reference product name, while the original catalogue provides a more precise description of this category. The full description in the catalogue is high-performance digital computers, electronic components, and related equipment, which includes specific types such as:

1. Digital computers with an adjusted peak performance (APP) greater than 8.0 Weighted TeraFLOPS
2. Electronic components specifically designed or modified to enhance performance, utilizing processor aggregation to achieve an APP greater than 8.0 Weighted TeraFLOPS

This distinction highlights that while the reference product names provide a general categorization, the original descriptions in the catalogue define the technical specifications that determine whether an item requires an export license.

Furthermore, on April 4, 2025, the Ministry of Commerce, in coordination with the General Administration of Customs, issued an announcement on implementing export control measures on seven types of medium and heavy rare earth-related items — specifically samarium (Sm), gadolinium (Gd), terbium (Tb), dysprosium (Dy), lutetium (Lu), scandium (Sc), and yttrium (Y). The measures took effect from the date of publication. Although rare-earth materials are not ICT goods, they are crucial in the production of various high-tech products, such as batteries, and display screends in electronic devices.

Furthermore, in 2017, the National Standardization Administration, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Commerce jointly issued the Guiding Opinions on Foreign-Funded Enterprises Participating in the Standardization Work of China, aiming to create a fair standardization environment for foreign-invested enterprises.

Specifically, Article 1 of the Guiding Opinions stipulates that foreign-invested enterprises participating in China’s standardization work shall enjoy equal treatment with domestic enterprises. Article 4 then states that foreign-invested enterprises may participate in the drafting of national standards and the translation of national standards into foreign languages. They may also provide opinions and suggestions during processes such as project initiation, solicitation of opinions, and implementation of standards.

law: Notice on Improving Tax Policies for Cross-Border E-Commerce Retail Imports 《关于完善跨境电子商务零售进口税收政策的通知》
impact: According to the Notice published by the Ministry of Finance, starting from Jan 1, 2019, the annual quota on cross-border e-commerce purchases for individual buyers will be raised from 20,000 to 26,000 yuan (about 3,566 USD). The limit on a single transaction will also be raised from 2,000 to 5,000 yuan (about 686 USD).

China's first comprehensive legislation governing e-commerce took effect on January 2019. The law applies to all 'e-commerce operators' including all natural and legal persons that engage in the business of selling merchandise and/or providing services on the internet or other information networks. This covers e-commerce platform operators, the vendors of goods and services on the e-commerce platforms of others, and those who operate their self-built websites or through other network services. The expanded wording is important as it covers non-traditional shopping channels including social media and messaging services such as WeChat and streaming sites such as Douyin. 

Article 12 states that E-commerce operators engaging in business activities that require relevant administrative licenses by law must obtain such licenses in accordance with the law.

The licenses that need to be obtained include both the Internet Content Provider (ICP) license and the Electroic Data Interchange (DEI) license.

According to Article 6 of the Measures for the Administration of Telecommunication Business Operation License, in order to obtain a DEI license, the following conditions must be met: (1) the operator must be a company legally established in accordance with the law; (2) it must have sufficient capital and professional personnel appropriate for its business activities; (3) it must have a good reputation or the capability to provide long-term services to users; (4) if operating within a province, autonomous region, or municipality, the minimum registered capital is RMB 1 million; if operating nationwide or across provinces, autonomous regions, or municipalities, the minimum registered capital is RMB 10 million; (5) it must have the necessary premises, facilities, and technical plans; (6) the company, its main investors, and key management personnel must not be listed on the telecom business dishonesty blacklist; and (7) other conditions as stipulated by the state.

Furthermore, According to Article 13 of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on Telecommunications, in order to obtain an ICP license, the following conditions must be met: (1) the operator must be a company legally established in accordance with the law; (2) it must have sufficient capital and professional personnel appropriate for its business activities; (3) it must have the credibility or capability to provide long-term services to users; and (4) other conditions as stipulated by the state.

As per the Public Procurement (Make in India) Order 2019 for Cyber Security Products, preference is granted to a company which is incorporated and registered in India or startup firms that meet the definition set out by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), provided the revenue from the product and IP licensing accrues to the firm in India. 

Types of cyber security products included in the notifications are anti-virus, cloud security, mobile security, firewall, OTP gateway, encryption subscription etc. The list of products can be found in the Public Procurement (Make in India) Order 2019 for Cyber Security Products.

law:
Government of India, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, Preference to Domestically Manufactured Electronic Products in Government Procurement, 2013;

Government of India, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, Guidelines for Providing Preference to Domestically Manufactured Electronic Products in Government Procurement, 2015
impact:
The Preferential Market Access (PMA) Policy provides that domestically manufactured equipment receives preferences in government procurement and in some types of private sector procurement. The underlying objectives are India’s goals to expand its domestic manufacturing capacity and to protect the security of its telecommunications networks. India revised the PMA in December 2013, but the revised policy continues to require that domestically manufactured goods constitute a certain percentage of the electronic products procured by government entities. Detailed guidelines on the implementation of the policy were issued in November 2015. 

The Notification stipulates that each Ministry or Department will satisfy a minimum percentage of their electronic product demand with local products which fulfil the minimum value addition prescribed for each item. The 2015 Guidelines provide that the minimum percentage of domestic procurement for any electronic product is 30%. The percentage of total procurement value for which preference is provided to domestic manufactured electronic products should be fixed so that competition is maximized while at the same time domestic manufacturing is encouraged. The 2013 Notification will be in operation for 10 years. 

The electronic products notified in the 2013 Notification include notebooks, tablets, desktop PCs, servers, printers, keyboards, monitors, USBs, ATMs, photocopiers, scanners, faxes, smartcards, mobile handsets, hand held terminals, PC projector, POS based services. The telecom products notified in the 2013 Notification include SIM Cards, encryption platforms, leased line network equipment, WiFi access systems etc.

law:
Government of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, General Circular No. 25/2014;

Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, FDI Policy 2020;
impact:
As per Para 5.2.15.3 of the FDI Policy [as amended vide Press Note 4 of 2019 and Press Note 1 of 2018] , 100% FDI is allowed in Single Brand Retail Trading (SBRT) under the automatic route subject to compliance of stipulated conditions. Para 5.2.15.3 (2) of the FDI Policy stipulates the following conditions for FDI in SBRT:
a) Products to be sold should be of a ‘Single Brand’ only.
b) Products should be sold under the same brand internationally i.e. products should be sold under the same brand in one or more countries other than India.
c) ‘Single Brand’ product-retail trading would cover only products which are branded during manufacturing.
d) A non-resident entity or entities, whether owner of the brand or otherwise, shall be permitted to undertake ‘single brand’ product retail trading in the country for the specific brand, either directly by the brand owner or through a legally tenable agreement executed between the Indian entity undertaking single brand retail trading and the brand owner.
e) In respect of proposals involving foreign investment beyond 51%, sourcing of 30% of the value of goods purchased, will be done from India, preferably from MSMEs, village and cottage industries, artisans and craftsmen, in all sectors. The quantum of domestic sourcing will be self-certified by the company, to be subsequently checked, by statutory auditors, from the duly certified accounts which the company will be required to maintain. This procurement requirement would have to be met, in the first instance, as an average of five years’ total value of the goods procured, beginning 1st April of the year of the commencement of SBRT business (i.e. opening of the first store or start of online retail, whichever is earlier). Thereafter, SBRT entity shall be required to meet the 30% local sourcing norms on an annual basis. For the purpose of ascertaining the sourcing requirement, the relevant entity would be the company, incorporated in India, which is the recipient of foreign investment for the purpose of carrying out single-brand product retail trading.
f) For the purpose of meeting local sourcing requirement laid down at para (e) above, all procurements made from India by the SBRT entity for that single brand shall be counted towards local sourcing, irrespective of whether the goods procured are sold in India or exported. SBRT entity is also permitted to set off sourcing of goods from India for global operations against the mandatory sourcing requirement of 30%. For this purpose, ‘sourcing of goods from India for global operations’ shall mean value of goods sourced from India for global operations for that single brand (in INR terms) in a particular financial year directly by the entity undertaking SBRT or its group companies (resident or non-resident), or indirectly by them through a third party under a legally tenable agreement.
g) An SBRT entity operating through brick and mortar stores can also undertake retail trading through e-commerce. However, retail trading through e-commerce can also be undertaken prior to opening of brick and mortar stores, subject to the condition that the entity opens brick and mortar stores within 2 years from date of start of online retail.

Conditions mentioned at Para 5.2.15.3 (2) (b) & 5.2.15.3 (2) (d) will not be applicable for undertaking SBRT of Indian brands. Indian brands should be owned and controlled by resident Indian citizens and/or companies which are owned and controlled by resident Indian citizens.

law:
Patents Act No.39 1970; 

Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Patent Rules (Amendment) 2003
impact:
In India, copyright, trademark, and patent applications can be filed online, while design applications require in-person or online filing (Copyright registration is not mandatory. Copyright is automatically granted to the creator). Regarding patents, applicants without a registered business in India must file through an Indian attorney or agent and provide an address for service in India as per Rule 5 of the Patents Rules, 2003 (as amended). This includes a postal and email address in India, which is essential for proceedings. Without this, the Controller is not obligated to act on applications or send notices.

The Patents Act, 1970 (as amended) and Patents Rules, 2003 (as amended) continue to mandate an address for service in India for filing patent applications, as reaffirmed in the Patent Rules Amendment, 2024, to protect applicant interests regardless of nationality.

Section 39 of the Patents Act, 1970 requires Indian residents to obtain prior written permission from the Controller to file patent applications abroad unless the same application is filed in India at least six weeks earlier. Violations result in deemed abandonment (Section 40), revocation of patents (Section 64), and penalties (Section 118). Permission requests are resolved within 21 days using a simple form (Form 25). These provisions apply only to Indian residents, not inventors, and remain unchanged in the Patent Rules Amendment, 2024, as they adequately safeguard applicant interests.

In section 107 A, the Patents Act states the actions that are not considered as infringements of patent rights. Moreover, there are mentions of remedies, civil and administrative procedures and provisional measures to deal with infringements. For example section (108) in the Patents Act list injunction, damages/ an account of profits and seizure, forfeiture and destruction of infringing goods as a possible relief(s) for infringement. law:

Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Patent Rules (Amendment) 2003
impact:
Indian Patent Act, 1970 (as amended) is a fully TRIPS compliant meeting all international obligations and simultaneously utilizing the flexibilities provided in the international regime to address its developmental concerns.

The Indian Patents Act maintains a fine balance between private rights on one hand and the rights of the society at large on other hands. In order to streamline processing of Intellectual Property Rights case, Delhi and Madras High Courts have created the Intellectual Property Division (IPD) to exclusively deal with all matters related to Intellectual Property Rights in line with global practices. Additionally, some High Court including the Bombay, Calcutta, and Gujarat High Courts have designated specialized IP benches. This has fast-tracked the disposal of IP cases including patent cases. In the first year of the establishment of IPD in Delhi High court (DHC-IPD), more than two-thirds of all the original petitions concerning patents transferred from the Appellate Board to the DHC-IPD have been disposed.

India currently follows the fair dealing model of copyright exceptions, in compliance with the three-step test and the copyright exceptions provided under  Chapter XI – Infringement of Copyright Section 52(1) (Certain acts not to be infringement of copyright) of the Copyright Act, 1957, a fair dealing with any work (not being a computer programme) for the purposes of private or personal use, criticism or review and the reporting of current events and current affairs does not constitute an infringement of copyright. This approach is fully in line with all international conventions under the International Copyright regime, including the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) of the World Trade Organization (WTO), the Berne Convention, 1886, the WIPO Copyright Treaty, 1996, the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty, 1996, the Beijing Treaty, 2012, and the Marrakesh Treaty for Access to Published Works for Visually Impaired and Print Disabled Persons, 2013, of which India is a member.

law: Copyright Act No.14 1957
impact:
In India, the Copyright Act of 1957 provides the legal framework for addressing copyright infringement, including online piracy. Section 51 of the Copyright Act defines infringement and provides that any person who, without a license granted by the owner of the copyright or the Registrar of Copyrights, or in contravention of the conditions of a license so granted or of any condition imposed by a competent authority under this Act, does anything, the exclusive right to do which is by this Act conferred upon the owner of the copyright, shall be deemed to infringe the copyright.

Section 55 of the Copyright Act empowers the courts to grant injunctions to prevent the infringement of copyright. It states that where the existence of the right to receive royalties in respect of any work has been established to the satisfaction of the court, the court may, in its discretion, grant an injunction to restrain the infringement of the right by the defendant or any agent of his or any person acting under his authority.

The District Level Commercial Courts and the Commercial Benches in all 25 High Courts of India have been set up under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015(as amended in 2018) and are functioning efficiently all over India. Moreover, the Delhi High Court has been at the forefront of addressing online copyright piracy through dynamic injunctions. In the landmark case of UTV Software Communications Ltd. v. 1337x.to, the court issued a dynamic injunction against various websites that were facilitating the unauthorized distribution of the plaintiff's copyrighted content. The court directed the blocking of these websites and also ordered that any new domain names or URLs used by these websites to infringe the plaintiff's copyright would also be covered by the injunction. Similarly, in the case of Sony Pictures Networks India Pvt. Ltd. v. the website known as 'dwatchseries.to,' the Delhi High Court granted a dynamic injunction restraining the website from hosting, streaming, reproducing, distributing, making available to the public, or communicating to the public any cinematograph work, sound recording, or musical work belonging to the plaintiff without authorization. In 2019, another recent case of  Star India Pvt. Ltd. v. Moviestrunk. Com, the High Court passed an order of injunction restraining the defendant websites from ‘unauthorizedly streaming, downloading, communicating or distributing the cinematograph film ‘Mission Mangal’, including any extracts or clippings thereof.The Honourable Court further directed IPTV providers and ISP to block the unlawful websites and the various government departments to issue notices to IPTV and ISP to block the said website.

These judgments highlight the effectiveness of dynamic injunctions in combating online copyright piracy. By granting injunctions that can adapt to the changing online landscape, courts can effectively protect the rights of copyright owners and deter infringers from engaging in piracy. Dynamic injunctions have emerged as a crucial tool in combating online copyright piracy, particularly in the digital age where infringing content can spread rapidly across the internet. Dynamic injunctions arise when a continuing injunction is issued, the specific targets of which are not mentioned in the primary order but rather an emphasis is laid on the impugned subject matter and protected rights, thereby including in its ambit any potential infringements. This legal mechanism allows courts to issue injunctions that can adapt to the evolving nature of online infringement, ensuring that they remain effective in addressing the challenges posed by digital piracy.

In India, there is no law as such for the issuance of “dynamic injunctions,” but in order to meet pressing needs, the courts are granting such injunctions by exercising their inherent powers under Section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908. Parties can implead the mirrored websites under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC. In order to reduce the burden on courts, the joint registrar of the Delhi High Court has been delegated the power to adjudicate upon the issue of the additional website being added to the existing blocking order.

law: Cinematograph (Amendment) Bill No. XlVI 2023
impact:
The lack of predictability around Section 31D and overly broad exceptions for certain uses have raised concerns about the strength of copyright protection in India. However, the Cinematograph (Amendment) Act, 2023, was passed by the Indian Parliament on August 4, 2023. The amendment addresses various issues relating to film certification, including the issue of unauthorized recording and exhibition of firms and film privacy by transmission of unauthorized copies on the Internet and imposes strict penalties for privacy. These amendments are in harmony with the existing laws that addresses the issue of film privacy, viz The Copyright Act, 1957 and the Information Technology Act (IT) 2000. 

The new sections 6AA and 6AB of the Act prohibit carrying out or abetting (i) the unauthorized recording and (ii) the unauthorized exhibition of films. Attempting an unauthorized recording will also be an offense. An unauthorized recording means making or transmitting an infringing copy of a film at a licensed place for film exhibition without the owner’s authorization. An unauthorized exhibition means the public exhibition of an infringing copy of the film for profit: (i) at a location not licensed to exhibit films; or (ii) in a manner that infringes upon the copyright law. The above offenses will be punishable under the amended Section 7 of the Act with: (i) imprisonment between three months and three years; and (ii) a fine between three lakh rupees and 5% of the audited gross production cost.

The Copyright (Amendment) Act, 2012 has aligned Indian copyright law with the minimum standards set forth in the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT) and WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT), commonly referred to as the WIPO Internet Treaties. India acceded to these treaties in 2018. The enforcement of these provisions relies on rights owners seeking assistance from Indian courts to protect their rights against online piracy of their copyrighted content based on the relevant Copyright Act provisions.

law: Information Technology Act No.21 2000
impact:
Article 69  (Power to issue directions for interception or monitoring or decryption of any information through any computer resource) of the Information Technology Act states that if the Controller is satisfied that it is necessary or expedient so to do in the interest of the sovereignty or integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign Stales or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence, for reasons to be recorded in writing, by order, direct any agency of the Government to intercept any information transmitted through any computer resource. The subscriber or any person incharge of the computer resource shall, when called upon by any agency which has been directed under sub-section (1), extend all facilities and technical assistance to decrypt the information. The subscriber or any person who fails to assist the agency referred to in sub-section (2) shall be punished with an imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years. According to the regulation, information includes data, text, images, sound, voice, codes, computer programmes, software and databases or micro film or computer generated micro fiche.

Moreover, under Section 69 of the Information Technology Act, the government is empowered to control, supervise, or monitor any information in the interest of its sovereign functions or the security of the state. The government is allowed to keep an eye on any information flowing through its state or affecting its citizens. The Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Interception, Monitoring, and Decryption of Information) Rules, 2009 (IT Rules), have laid down the procedure for the above.

impact:
There is no stand-alone trade secret law in India at present. However, in India the trade secrets and confidential information are protected under the principles of equity, tort law, and common law principles of breach of confidence, etc. Indian courts have also applied Section 27 of the Contract Act, which deals with the restraint of trade, while addressing the issue of infringement of trade secrets by employees of companies as per the non-disclosure agreements.

As per the decision of  Delhi High Court in 1995, a trade secret is defined as any information with commercial value, which is not available in the public domain and the disclosure of which would cause significant harm to the owner. Although there is no specific law or enactment on trade secrets in India, the Indian courts and tribunals have upheld protection of trade secrets under other laws such as contact law, copyright law, principles of equity and common law action of breach of confidence (which is basically breach of an obligation to keep a piece information secret). 

In addition to the above, the Information Technology law of 2000 also sets legal means of protection to confidential information in the form of the electronic records (Article 10 Power to make rules by Central Government in respect of digital signature). It is reported that India’s National Intellectual Property Rights Policy called for trade secrets to serve as an “important area of study for future policy development,” in 2016 but India appears to have not yet prioritized this work.

law: Calcutta High Court in the Fairfest Media Ltd vs Lte Group Plc and Ors 2015
impact:
The ruling of the Calcutta High Court claims: whatever its source may be, a person who has obtained information in confidence is not allowed to use it as a springboard for activities harmful to the person who made the confidential communication. According to the High Court in the Fairfest Media Ltd vs Lte Group Plc and Ors, (2015), a party may not utilize information it obtained in confidence to harm the party it recieved said information from. The ruling in this case added to the already vast court upheld protections of trade secrets.

The "springboard doctrine" is a legal principle that prohibits improper use of trade secret information, such as theft or breach of confidence, to gain an unfair competitive advantage, even if the information is not protected by intellectual property rights. The springboard doctrine in India prohibits improper use of trade secret information to gain a competitive advantage over the rightful owner. Its application may vary depending on the specific facts and circumstances of each case. Courts will consider factors such as the nature of the information, how it was obtained, and the extent of the unfair advantage gained by the party using the information.

law: Amendment in Unified License relating to infrastructure sharing and Public Wi-Fi services
impact:
The amendment in License Conditions to allow active infrastructure sharing, inclding core Networks, between telecom operators, which will reduce costs and enhance roll out of services - Cellular Operators Association in India. Sharing of Active infrastructure amongst Service Providers based on the mutual agreements entered amongst them is permitted. Active infrastructure sharing will be limited to antenna, feeder cable, Node B, Radio Access Network (RAN) and transmission system only. This includes Internet Service. However, there are limitations on the sharing which are not stated within the amendment. The Licensee may share its own active and passive infrastructure for providing other services authorized to it under any other telecom license issued by Licensor

Moreover, as per Unified License, infrastructure sharing is enabled. The relevant clauses of Unified License are given below: 
33. Sharing of infrastructure:
33.1 Sharing of active/passive infrastructure shall be governed by the terms and conditions of respective service authorization and amendment/guidelines to be issued by the Licensor from time to time.
33.2 Sharing of Active infrastructure amongst Service Providers based on the mutual agreements entered amongst them is permitted. Active infrastructure sharing will be limited to antenna, feeder cable, Node B, Radio Access Network (RAN) and transmission system only. Sharing of infrastructure related to Wi-Fi equipment such as Wi-Fi router, Access Point etc. is allowed. Sharing of backhaul is also permitted.
33.3 The Licensee may share its own active and passive infrastructure for providing other services authorized to it under any other telecom license issued by Licensor. Other clauses related to infrastructure are mentioned in Chapters of other services in Unified license [Chapter VIII for Access Service: Clause no. 2.1(a)(ii), Chapter IX for Internet Service: Clause no. 2.1(i)].
