law: Reserve Bank of India Directive 2018
impact:
In April 2018, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a one-page directive  vide circular DPSS.CO.OD.No 2785/06.08.005/2017-18  stating that, within six months, all payment data held by payment companies should be held in local facilities. The Directive noted that this would help the RBI gain "unfettered supervisory access" to transaction data, which it needs to ensure proper monitoring.
 
Following a negative response from international payment companies such as MasterCard, Visa and American Express, the RBI has proposed (in "Frequently Asked Questions" of its website) to ease this restriction, so as to allow payment firms to store data offshore, as long as a copy was kept in India. The RBI has further clarified that for cross border transaction data consisting of a foreign component and domestic component, a copy of the domestic component may be stored abroad, if required. 

With respect to processing of payment transactions outside India, the RBI requires that the data must be stored only in India after processing and should be deleted from systems abroad and brought back to India no later than 24 hours after processing. Any subsequent activity such as settlement processing after payment processing done outside India, this must be undertaken on a real time basis pursuant to which the data must be stored only in India. 

The RBI has clarified that banks, especially foreign banks, can continue to store banking data abroad but in respect of domestic payment transactions, the data must be stored only in India.
note:
The legal part written herein is accurate. In April 2018, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a, mandating all payment system providers to ensure that the entire data related to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India. The Directive noted that this would help the RBI gain "unfettered supervisory access" to transaction data, which would ensure better monitoring. 

RBI has clarified that for cross-border transaction data, consisting of a foreign component and a domestic component, a copy of the domestic component may be stored abroad if required. Further it was clarified that there is no bar on processing payment transactions outside India if so desired by the PSOs. However, the data shall be stored only in India after the processing. The complete end-to-end transaction details should be part of the data.

With respect to the processing of payment transactions outside India, the RBI requires that the data must be stored only in India after processing and should be deleted from systems abroad and brought back to India no later than one business day or 24 hours from payment processing, whichever is earlier. Any subsequent activity, such as settlement processing after payment processing done outside India, must be undertaken on a real-time basis, pursuant to which the data must be stored only in India. 

The RBI has clarified that in case of banks, especially foreign banks, earlier specifically permitted to store the banking data abroad, they may continue to do so; however, in respect of domestic payment transactions, the data shall be stored only in India.

The directive is issued under Section 10(2) read with Section 18 of Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007

law:
Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules 2011;

Clarification on Information Technology (Reasonable security practices and procedures and sensitive personal data or information) Rules 2011
impact:
Rule 6 of the Information Technology Rules 2011 provides that cross-border data transfers of sensitive personal data or information can be made to any other corporate entity or person in India or to any other country that ensures the same level of data protection as provided under the Rules. Disclosure of sensitive personal data or information by a corporation to any third party shall require prior permission from the provider of such information, who has provided such information under lawful contract or otherwise, unless such disclosure has been agreed to in the contract between the body corporate and provider of information, or where the disclosure is necessary for compliance of a legal obligation. Sensitive personal information includes passwords, financial information such as bank account or credit/debit card details, sexual orientation, physical, mental health condition, biometric information etc.

According to the Clarification on Information Technology Rules, published in August 2011, corporations providing services relating to collection, storage, dealing or handling of sensitive personal data or information under contractual obligation with any legal entity located within or outside India are not subject to the requirement of Rule 6.

law:
Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015
impact:
As per the SEBI Listing Regulations, a listed entity (i.e. an entity which is listed on the stock market) is required to have a policy for the preservation of documents. The SEBI Listing Regulations require that records, books, papers and documents of the company be preserved as per the following classifications:
i) Schedule I - to be preserved permanently. Documents listed under these schedule include incorporation documents, share certificates, register of minutes of board meetings, register of members etc. 
ii) Schedule II – to be preserved for eight years. Documents listed under this schedule include books of accounts, attendance register of board meetings, register of debenture holders etc.
iii) Schedule III – to be preserved for a minimum period of five years or such higher period as may be determine by the board of directors of the company. Documents listed under this schedule include register of stock options, register of directors and key managerial personnel, disclosures made under applicable company laws etc. 
As per the SEBI Listing Regulations, documents set out in Schedule I and II can be kept in electronic mode. The complete list of documents under each schedule is set out in the SEBI Listing Regulations.

any computer resource) of the Information Technology Act 2000, as amended by the Information Technology (Amendment) Act 2008, gives the central and state governments the power to direct any agency to intercept, monitor or decrypt, or cause to be intercepted, monitored or decrypted any information transmitted, received or stored through any computer resources. law: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021
impact:
Under Part II Due Diligence by Intermediaries and Grievance Redressal Mechanism, Rule 3 Due diligence by an intermediary, the Information Technology Rules provide that an intermediary, after receiving 'actual knowledge' through a court order or by being notified by a government agency must remove information that is prohibited by law in relation to the interest and sovereignty of India, the security of the state, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence or information which violates any law which is in force. Such information has to be removed within a duration of thirty six hours from receipt of actual knowledge by the intermediary. 

Significant Social Media Intermediaries, defined as having more than 5 million registered Indian users, need to observe additional due diligence requirements to claim the immunity/safe harbour available. Rule 6 of the Information Technology Rules provides that even if a social media intermediary does not meet this user-threshold, the Central Government may still require an intermediary to meet these additional obligations if it believes that their operations create a material risk of harm to the sovereignty and integrity of India or to the security of the State. This discretion to the Central government may lead to the arbitrary imposition of additional obligations on certain intermediaries. The additional due diligence requirements include appointing certain personnel for compliance, enabling identification of the first originator of the information on its platform under certain conditions, and deploying technology-based measures on a best-effort basis to identify certain types of content.
timeframe: Since February 2021, last amended in April 2023

law:
The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code)
Rules, 2021
impact:
India amended its IT law on to prohibit Facebook, Twitter and other social media firms from publishing, hosting or sharing false or misleading information about “any business” of the government and said the firms will be required to rely on New Delhi’s own fact-check unit to determine the authenticity of any claim.

Under part II "Due Diligence by Intermediaries and Grievance Redressal Mechanism" section 3(1) (b) point v states that deceives or misleads the addressee about the origin of the message or knowingly and intentionally communicates any misinformation or information which is patently false and untrue or misleading in nature [or is identified as fake or false by the fact check unit at the Press Information Bureau of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting or other agency authorised by the Central Government for fact checking or, in respect of any business of the Central Government, by its department in which such business is transacted under the rules of business made under clause (3) of article 77 of the Constitution]

Failure to comply with the rule, which also impacts internet service providers such as Jio and Airtel, risks the firms losing their safe harbor protections. The rule assigns a unit of the government arbitrary and over-broad powers to determine the authenticity of online content and bypasses the principles of natural justice. The notification of these amended rules cement the chilling effect on the fundamental right to speech and expression, particularly on news publishers, journalists, activists, etc. The fact check unit could effectively issue a takedown order to social media platforms and even other intermediaries across the internet stack, potentially bypassing the process statutorily prescribed under the Section 69A (Power to issue directions for blocking for public access of any information through any computer resource) of the IT Act, 2000.

law: Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Foreign Direct Investment Policy Circular 2016, 2017, 2020
impact:
Under section 5.2.15.2 .3 (i) in all amendements India permits up to 100 percent Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in business-to-business (“marketplace-based”) electronic commerce, i.e. "providing of an information technology platform by an e-commerce entity on a digital & electronic network to act as a facilitator between buyer and seller." However, under (ii) India prohibits foreign investment in business-to-consumer (or “inventory-based”) electronic commerce, also defined as "e-commerce activity where inventory of goods and services is owned by e-commerce entity and is sold to the consumers directly". 

As per section 5.2.15.2.2 (iii) in all amendements , when a marketplace e-commerce entity exercises ownership or control over the inventory, the business is categorized into the inventory-based model. Additionally, India implemented regulations that expressly prohibit subsidiaries of foreign-owned marketplace-based electronic commerce sites from selling products on their parent companies’ sites. The rules also prohibit exclusivity arrangements by which electronic commerce retailers can offer a product on an exclusive basis. 

As per 2017 amendment, section 5.2.5.2, the only exceptions for FDI in inventory-based electronic commerce are for food-product retailing and single-brand retailers that meet certain conditions, including the operation of physical stores in India. Since 2020, under section 5.2.15.3 (g) of the 2020 amendment the FDI policy stipulates that retail trading through e-commerce can also be undertaken prior to opening physical stores, subject to the condition that the entity opens physical stores within two years from the date of start of online retail. Overall, it is reported that these narrow exceptions limit the ability of many electronic commerce service suppliers to serve the Indian market.

impact:

law: Regulation of the Minister of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia No.41/PER/M.KOMINFO/10/2009 on Procedures for Assessing the Achievement of Domestic Component Levels in the Implementation of Telecommunications 2009
impact:
Decree No. 41/PER/M.KOMINFO/10/2009: Article 1(4) and subsequent sections define and outline the procedures for assessing domestic content (TKDN) in telecommunications.
Article 1(4): Definition of Level of Domestic Component (TKDN). TKDN (LDC) is defined as the portion of domestic components in goods, services, or a combination of both, used in telecommunications.
It includes:
- Goods: Telecommunication materials and equipment.
- Services: Design, engineering, and other supporting services.
- Combination: A mix of goods and services.
The domestic component must involve local manufacturing, fabrication, assembling, work settlement, and services performed domestically, using local experts and software.

Article 3(1) and 3(2) of Calculation of TKDN and Foreign Component provides the formula for calculating the Level of Domestic Component (TKDN) and explicitly identifies the Foreign Component (FC) as part of the calculation. The formulas are:

Formula 1:
% TKDN (Capex) = ((Total Capex − Foreign Component Capex) /Total Capex) × 100 %

Formula 2:
% TKDN (Capex) = (Domestic Component Capex / Total Capex) ×100%

This explicitly separates foreign components (e.g., imported goods, foreign services, foreign software) from domestic components, ensuring that foreign elements are excluded from the TKDN percentage.

Article 4(1) and 4(2) of Proof of Domestic Expenditure requires telecommunication providers to show proof of domestic expenditure for telecommunication materials/equipment sourced from domestic vendors. It also mandates that the percentage of TKDN for these materials/equipment must be authenticated by:
- An authorized agency or
- An independent survey institute assigned by the government.
This ensures that foreign components are excluded unless they are explicitly verified as domestic.

Article 5 of Verification of Domestic Components  mandates that any assessment of TKDN using telecommunication materials/equipment from domestic providers must be verified by:
- An authorized agency, or
- An independent survey institute.
This verification process ensures that foreign components are not misrepresented as domestic.

Article 6 of Local Content Threshold states that telecommunication materials/equipment with ≥ 50% local content are considered to have 100% local content for TKDN purposes. This provision effectively excludes foreign components from being counted as domestic unless they meet the 50% threshold.

law: Regulation of the Minister of Industry No. 15/M-IND/PER/3/2016 on Specification Standards and Price Standards for Domestic Transmission Towers and Conductors to Accelerate the Development of Electricity Infrastructure 2016
impact:

The specifications and pricing standards are likely designed to favor domestic products, indirectly excluding foreign goods that do not align with these standards.

Article 4 establishes a benchmark pricing system for the procurement of domestic Transmission Towers and Conductors. This ensures that public procurement adheres to fair and consistent pricing, avoiding overpricing or underpricing. By mandating adherence to Standard Prices for domestic products, Article 4 indirectly excludes foreign products that may not align with these price benchmarks. This is because foreign products are not explicitly included in the pricing standards, and the regulation prioritizes domestic goods. The Standard Prices are tied to the domestic content requirements (TKDN) outlined in Article 6. 

Article 6 article mandates that Tower Transmission and Conductor products used in the acceleration of electricity infrastructure must meet a minimum Tingkat Komponen Dalam Negeri (TKDN) (Domestic Component Level) of 40%. Article 7: The TKDN value must be verified and certified through a formal process, as outlined in this article. Ensuring that only products meeting the domestic content requirements are eligible for procurement, further excluding foreign products that fail to meet these standards.

law: Law No. 25 on Investment 2007
impact:
Indonesia's Investment Law No. 25 of 2007 provides a broad legal framework for investment in Indonesia, emphasizing openness and equal treatment to foreign investment (Article 6) while allowing for specific restrictions in certain sectors. For precise foreign equity limits in sectors relevant to digital trade, one would need to refer to the Positive Investment List and the Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021. The “Positive Investment List,” is part of Indonesia’s broader strategy to attract foreign investment while protecting specific sectors for local businesses. The Positive Investment List allows 100% foreign ownership in several key areas to encourage foreign investment in digital infrastructure and technology (listed in the annexes). 

This includes large-scale e-commerce platforms, classified under high-capital investment thresholds, which enable global players to operate independently, and data centers (Business Field No. 63111), which are critical for supporting Indonesia’s digital economy and data storage needs. Additionally, cloud computing services for general use are open to full foreign ownership, allowing flexibility for international technology companies to provide cloud services in Indonesia. Over-the-top (OTT) digital content platforms, such as video and music streaming services, are also unrestricted, promoting the growth of diverse content services for Indonesian consumers. These policies align with Indonesia’s digital transformation goals by enhancing technology transfer, infrastructure development, and consumer access to global digital services, while maintaining regulatory oversight for sectors with more strategic or sensitive data requirements, such as critical infrastructure and payment systems.

This includes foreign participation to SOEs in telecommunication and delivery service sectors (as regulated in the Government Regulation No. 15/2013 amended by the Government Regulation No.41/2021).

The Government Regulation No. 15 of 2013, as amended by Government Regulation No. 41 of 2021, regulates the foreign ownership limit for State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) and their subsidiaries. This regulation emphasizes maintaining government majority control in strategic sectors. The 49% cap is designed to attract foreign investment and expertise while keeping majority ownership within the Indonesian government.

The Telecommunications and Delivery Service  sectors are classified as “strategic sectors” that are subject to heightened restrictions due to their importance to national security and public access. On one hand, Indonesia protects access to public procurement as a tool to support domestic industries and secure government-controlled projects for local players. On the other hand, it opens select SOEs to foreign ownership, recognizing the value of international capital and expertise in strengthening public-sector entities without relinquishing majority government control. In 2020, Indonesia issued the Omnibus Law 2020 (as amended by the Regulation in Lieu of Law No. 2 of 2022 on Job Creation) that removes the possibility for the Indonesian government to block foreign investments based on national interest considerations. The regulation states that all sectors are open for foreign investments except the sectors that are close for foreign investments such as chemical weapons, substances harming ozone, narcotics, gambling activities, fishery activities related to Annex 1 of CITEs,  and corrals. None of these sectors are related to digital and computer services.

The Omnibus Law 2023, known as Law No. 6 of 2023, builds upon the previous Omnibus Law enacted in 2020, aiming to further streamline regulations and enhance the investment climate in Indonesia. This law introduces significant reforms to simplify business licensing processes, reduce bureaucratic hurdles, and promote foreign direct investment across various sectors. It emphasizes the government's commitment to creating a more favorable environment for investors by ensuring that all sectors are generally open to foreign investment, except for those explicitly restricted, such as industries related to chemical weapons, narcotics, and certain environmental concerns. The Omnibus Law 2023 reflects Indonesia's strategic approach to attract foreign capital while balancing national interests, particularly in sectors deemed sensitive or critical to national security.

Article 12 of the Omnibus Law 2023 states that all business sectors are open to foreign investment, except for those explicitly closed to foreign investment. This indicates a more liberal approach to foreign investment, reducing the scope for screening based on national interest considerations. Article 13 outlines the sectors that are closed to foreign investment, which include specific industries such as narcotics, gambling, and certain environmental concerns. Article 76 (reinfored by Article 77) of the Omnibus Law emphasizes simplifying investment requirements and procedures, which aligns with the government's goal of attracting foreign investment and reducing bureaucratic hurdles.

However, it is important to understand that no mandatory local representation requirement for non-PCT patent applications under Indonesian regulations. The explicit requirement for local representation applies only to PCT applications.

Fees are defined in Article 37(5) and Article 45. These provisions outline various fees including transmittal fees, search fees, and page-excess fees, which may increase the cost substantially, especially for complex applications.

Article 3(2) (Article 3(2)) states that patent applications must be submitted in Bahasa Indonesia. Additionally, if documents are initially in a foreign language, Article 17(6) requires that translations for the title, description, claims, and abstract be provided in Bahasa Indonesia within 30 days of filing. Failure to provide these translations will result in the application being considered withdrawn.

The provisions for international priority claims align with the Paris Convention, as specified in Permenkumham Nomor 38 Tahun 2018, Article 36(1). This article confirms that an application claiming priority must be submitted within 12 months from the priority date. If the deadline is not met, the priority right is forfeited, which could impact the application’s precedence over similar filings.

The Patent Law Number 13 of 2016 mandates a Local Agent (Kuasa), Article 1, No. 7 (Article 1, No. 7) specifies that a local intellectual property consultant or agent is mandatory for filing if the applicant is represented by someone other than themselves.

A Local Filing Requirement is outlined in Article 46 of Undang-Undang Nomor 13 Tahun 2016 as amended by UU Nomor 65 Tahun 2024, applicants are required to file patents in Indonesia within a specific time frame if claiming priority rights. This impacts applicants who intend to file abroad first, as it imposes a procedural prerequisite to file domestically.

A concerpt of claiming priority, Article 30 of Law Number 65 of 2024 which is the Third Amendment to Law Number 13 of 2016 on Patents, an applicant who wishes to claim priority under the Paris Convention must file the patent in Indonesia within 12 months of the original filing date in another country. If this 12-month period is missed, the application may still be filed within an additional 4-month grace period, but this requires payment of additional fees.

impact:
In Indonesia's current legislation covers civil and administrative remedies and provisional measures in the context of patent enforcement and protection. 

Article 47 (UU Nomor 13 Tahun 2016) allows for substantive examination procedures. Article 132 (UU Nomor 13 Tahun 2016) provides the basis for filing civil suits for patent infringement. However, these civil provisions do not specify expedited civil relief or injunctions within standard procedures, indicating a lack of structured civil remedies aimed explicitly at rapid enforcement. Thus,  provides only the right for patent holders to initiate civil lawsuits for damages due to patent infringement, covering civil remedies.

UU Nomor 65 Tahun 2024 (the latest amendment to the patent law) details administrative processes. There are limited administrative pathways, such as appeals to the Patent Appeal Commission (Komisi Banding Paten) for specific decisions, but this is not equivalent to the broader administrative enforcement seen in some other jurisdictions. Article 120, UU Nomor 65 Tahun 2024 includes the option for administrative action by the Directorate General of Intellectual Property (DGIP), which oversees patent administration but does not specify immediate administrative remedies for enforcement. 

Essentially, in Indonesia, legal remedies concerning intellectual property - particularly through litigation - are submitted to the Commercial Court. as of now, there are no specific procedural rules governing proceedings in the Commercial Court, so cases continue to follow the general civil procedure law. 

Additionally, provisional measures are explicitly provided for under Law Number 13 of 2016 on Patents, which remains in effect. The Law provides a mechanism for provisional or emergency measures in responsee to potential or ongoing patent infringements. Specifically, Chapter XIV on PROVISIONAL DETERMINATION BY THE COURT, in Article 155, which states: 
At the request of the party suffering losses due to the implementation of the Patent, the Commercial Court may issue a provisional determination to:
a.	prevent the entry of goods suspected of infringing the Patent and/or related rights.
b.	secure and prevent the removal of evidence by alleged infringer; and/or
c.	halt the infringement in order to prevent further losses.
note:
Indonesia's intellectual property (IP) enforcement is mainly governed by civil law, providing remedies like judicial procedures and injunctions. However, its patent laws lack specific provisions for effective administrative remedies and civil injunctions for patent enforcement. Recent amendments have improved procedures but still need to sufficiently address the need for swift, patent-specific remedies to prevent infringement. While Indonesia complies with TRIPS by requiring provisional measures such as preliminary injunctions, their practical application is limited. Civil IP suits can be filed in the Commercial Court, which can issue provisional measures, but these processes are more streamlined than in other jurisdictions. Although the government is working to enhance IP enforcement through regional agreements like RCEP and the ASEAN IP Action Plan, implementation could have been faster, especially regarding patent issues.

The Indonesian government is working to improve digital IP enforcement through collaborations with online platforms and regulatory updates, such as the 2019 Electronic Information and Transactions regulation and MOCI’s guidelines. However, comprehensive, sector-wide tools for IP enforcement in digital spaces are still in development, affecting all IP owners operating in Indonesia’s large digital economy.

The Indonesian copyright law, primarily governed by Law No. 28 of 2014 concerning Copyright, has been criticized for not adequately addresses ing the complexities of digital content and user-generated content (UGC). A recent (February 29, 2024) ruling by the Indonesian Constitutional Court (case Number 84/PUU-XXI/2023) declared Article 10 of this law unconstitutional because it did not provide sufficient protection for UGC platforms, highlighting a significant gap in the legal framework that fails to keep pace with technological advancements (Article 10 of the Copyright Law: Managers of business premises are prohibited from allowing the sale and/or reproduction of goods resulted from Copyrights and/or Related Rights infringements in the location under their management. ) The Court found that the law's narrow focus on physical trading places excluded digital platforms, creating a legal gap that allowed copyright violations to persist without adequate enforcement. This lack of a comprehensive copyright framework and exceptions to address technological advancements violated the constitutional rights of creators to fair legal protection and economic benefits. The decision emphasized the need for updated regulations to ensure digital platforms prevent and address copyright violations effectively

Article 2: Specifies the scope of the law, stating that it applies to all works created by Indonesian nationals, residents, and legal entities, as well as foreign works published in Indonesia.
Article 3: Outlines the types of works protected under the law, including literary, artistic, and scientific works.
Article 4: Discusses the exclusive rights of authors, which include the right to reproduce, distribute, and publicly perform their works.
Article 5: Details the moral rights of authors, which include the right to attribution and the right to object to derogatory treatment of their works.

law: Law No.28 on Copyright 2014
impact:
In Indonesian Copyright Law (UU Nomor 28 Tahun 2014) contains several provisions regarding the enforcement of online copyright, specifically in terms of civil and administrative procedures, remedies, and provisional measures:

- Civil Remedies: Article 95 allows copyright holders to seek damages and pursue civil action against infringers, including online copyright violations. The article provides for compensation if copyright or related rights are infringed upon, covering both economic and moral rights. Article 95 provides copyright holders the right to pursue civil action for damages.

- Administrative Procedures: Article 49 mandates that the Directorate General of Intellectual Property (DGIP) in Indonesia oversees copyright protection and can coordinate with other agencies for enforcement. This coordination extends to digital platforms, though there is limited specificity about procedural details or administrative recourse for immediate action. Articles 54 and 55 establish government mechanisms to monitor and prevent digital copyright infringement, including through reporting systems and technological controls. Article 113 allows authorities to impose sanctions on those who facilitate or conduct unauthorized reproduction and distribution of copyrighted works, which could include digital content shared online.

- Provisional Measures: Article 98/99 allows copyright holders to request the court to issue provisional measures, including the cessation of alleged infringing acts, to prevent ongoing harm. This could theoretically apply to online copyright violations, although the practicality of obtaining quick provisional relief is limited by procedural complexity. Article 106: Allows the Commercial Court to issue provisional measures upon request from the aggrieved party. These measures can include preventing the entry of goods suspected of copyright infringement into the trade channels, withdrawing and seizing infringing goods, and preventing further infringement to avoid greater losses, fulfilling the requirement for interim relief.

- Provisions for Enforcement: Article 72 and Article 73 cover digital copyright infringements and permit the blocking of infringing online content, working through the Ministry of Communication and Informatics (MOCI) for enforcement in online environments. Article 107: Details the requirements for requesting provisional measures, such as providing evidence of copyright ownership and initial indications of infringement. Additionnally, Article 105 states that the right to file a civil lawsuit for copyright infringement does not preclude the right to pursue criminal charges, highlighting the dual avenues for enforcement.

It is also reported that enforcement officials often ask rights holders to pay for the raids. There are no provisions governing the disclosure of trade secrets (including source code) in the context of trade conducted through electronic systems under Government Regulation Number 80 of 2019 or Minister of Trade Regulation Number 31 of 2023. Government Regulation No.82 of 2012 as replaced by the Government Regulation No.71/2019 requires that providers of bespoke software provide or escrow the source codes associated with their service.

In Indonesia, the mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, including source code and algorithms, is primarily governed by the Law No. 30 of 2000 on Trade Secrets and Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012 on the Implementation of Electronic Systems and Transactions. While there is no broad requirement for mandatory disclosure of trade secrets in Indonesia. 

Law No. 30 of 2000 on Trade Secrets:
Article 1: Defines trade secrets and establishes the criteria for what constitutes a trade secret, emphasizing that it must be kept confidential and not generally known to the public.
Article 3: States that trade secrets are protected as long as they are kept confidential and have economic value. This implies that there is no general requirement for mandatory disclosure unless specified by law.
Article 11: Allows the holder of a trade secret to file a lawsuit against anyone who unlawfully discloses or uses the trade secret. This reinforces the idea that trade secrets should not be disclosed without consent.
Article 14 implies that a violation occurs if someone obtains or controls a trade secret in a manner contrary to the law.
Article 17 states that any person who deliberately and without rights uses the trade secret of another party, or conducts any acts as referred to in Article 13 or Article 14, can be sentenced to imprisonment of up to 2 years and/or a fine of up to 300 million rupiah.

Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012:
Article 8: Requires providers of electronic systems to submit source code and documentation to the relevant government agency when developing software for public institutions. 
Article 9: Mandates that providers must ensure the confidentiality of the source code used in their systems, indicating that while there may be a requirement to disclose to certain authorities, the confidentiality of that information must still be maintained.
Article 29: States that for criminal proceedings, electronic system providers must provide information contained in their systems upon lawful request from investigators.
The regulation does not impose any mandatory disclosure of trade secrets. Instead, it provides strong protections to ensure that the confidentiality of trade secrets is maintained during administrative, investigative, and legal processes.

Government Regulation No. 71 of 2019
Article 9: Developers of software specifically created for Penyelenggara Sistem Elektronik Lingkup Publik (Public Sector Electronic System Providers) are required to submit the source code and documentation of the software to the relevant public institution or agency.
If the public institution or agency does not have the infrastructure to store the source code, the developer must submit it to a trusted third party (source code escrow).
The developer must ensure that the source code and documentation are accessible to the trusted third party and guarantee its confidentiality. The source code is to be used only for the purposes of the public sector entity.

law: Law No.30 on Trade Secret 2000
impact:
Indonesia has a specific law (Law No. 30 of 2000) that defines trade secrets, outlines the rights of trade secret holders, and provides mechanisms for protection and enforcement. This indicates that there is a legal framework in place. The law provides clear definitions of what constitutes a trade secret and the conditions under which it is protected. Trade Secrets are legally defined as information in the field of technology and/or business that is not known by the public and has economic values as it is useful in business activities, and the confidentiality of which is maintained by its owner (Article 1). Trade secrets are protected as long as they are kept confidential and have economic value. This implies that there is no general requirement for mandatory disclosure unless specified by law (Article 3). It includes provisions Rights of Trade Secret Holders: Owners have the right to use, license, or prevent unauthorized use of their trade secrets (Articles 4 and 6). And the law allows trade secret holders to seek legal remedies against unauthorized disclosure or use (Articles 11 and 12). 

The law includes specific provisions regarding the rights of trade secret holders, the conditions for protection, and the legal recourse available in cases of infringement. Any person who deliberately and without rights uses the Trade Secret of another party, or conducts any acts as referred to in Article 13 or Article 14 of Law No. 30 shall be sentenced to imprisonment of at most 2 (two) years and/or a fine (Article 17). 

However, the law lacks implementing regulations, and there is no discovery procedure provided. As a result, certain aspects—such as the mechanism or parameters for proving violations—are not yet clearly regulated. The effectiveness of these provisions can vary in practice, indicating that while there is a framework, it may not be fully effective in all situations. The Law does not explicitly mention the lack of a discovery procedure, but it is a known issue in many legal systems that do not have robust discovery processes. This can make it difficult to prove that a trade secret was unlawfully obtained, especially if the suspected party had a prior relationship or access to the trade secret.

law: Law No.11 on Job Creation 2020
impact:
The Omnibus Law 2020 (as amended by the Regulation in Lieu of Law No. 2 of 2022 on Job Creation) requires business players with “passive infrastructure” used for telecommunications service activities to share access to such infrastructure with other telecommunications operators. “Passive infrastructure” includes ducting, towers, poles and other infrastructure that can be used for telecommunications networks. The central government and regional governments may participate in the development of passive infrastructure for common use by telecommunications operators.

The Omnibus Law (specifically Law Number 11 of 2020 on Job Creation) does mandate the sharing of passive telecommunications infrastructure in Indonesia. The Omnibus Law aims to streamline regulations and promote investment in various sectors, including telecommunications. It encourages the sharing of infrastructure to reduce costs and improve service delivery.

Article 15 specifically addresses the sharing of telecommunications infrastructure, stating that telecommunications operators are required to cooperate in the utilization of passive infrastructure. This includes sharing towers, ducts, and other facilities to enhance efficiency and reduce redundancy in infrastructure development. The law provides a framework for the government to establish regulations that facilitate infrastructure sharing. This includes setting standards for cooperation and ensuring that all operators have fair access to shared infrastructure.
timeframe: Since November 2020, last amended in November 2022
note: While the law mandates sharing, the actual implementation has faced challenges, including resistance from some operators who prefer to maintain their own infrastructure. The effectiveness of this mandate depends on regulatory enforcement and the willingness of operators to collaborate.

impact:
Indonesia regulations promote infrastructure sharing.  

Government Regulation Number 52 of 2000 on Telecommunications Operations:
This regulation doesn't directly address passive infrastructure sharing. However, the overarching goal of promoting efficient telecommunications operations (Article 1, point 8 and other articles) implicitly supports infrastructure sharing as a means to achieve efficiency.  The lack of specific mention highlights the regulatory gap that existed before more recent legislation.

Government Regulation Number 46 of 2021 on Post, Telecommunications, and Broadcasting:
This regulation doesn't have a dedicated article on passive infrastructure sharing, Article 22 discusses passive infrastructure.
Article 22: This article mentions passive infrastructure (points a-e) and allows for cooperation between network operators and passive infrastructure providers (point 1). It emphasizes fair and cost-based utilization (point 4) and allows the Minister to set upper limits on utilization prices if necessary (point 6). This shows a more proactive approach to encouraging passive infrastructure sharing compared to the 2000 regulation. However, it still relies on cooperation rather than direct mandates.

Regulation of Minister of Communications and Informatics Number 5 of 2021 on Telecommunications Operations:
This regulation delves deeper into the practical aspects of infrastructure sharing, particularly passive infrastructure.
Article 20 - Article 32: This section extensively covers the provision and utilization of passive infrastructure. It mandates that passive infrastructure providers open access to Telecommunications Operators (Article 23), outlines the principles of fair and non-discriminatory cooperation (Article 21), and details the process of determining reasonable tariffs (Article 28-31). It establishes a framework for cooperation and tariff setting, aiming to facilitate sharing.

While these articles establish a framework for cooperation and access, they do not explicitly mandate that all passive infrastructure must be shared. Instead, they set conditions and requirements for how such sharing should be conducted if it occurs. The emphasis is on ensuring fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory access, rather than imposing an outright obligation to share all passive infrastructure.
note:
Further regulations encourage passive infrastructure sharing through cooperation and the establishment of fair pricing mechanisms.  

It is important to note that Foreign investors are not allowed to own base stations/cellular towers. Given this regulation, foreign companies could be forced to exit the market as in the case of Singapore Singtel. (http://www.pwc.com/id/en/publications/assets/thereport_indonesia2012_obg.pdf)

law: Law No.36 on Telecommunications 1999
impact: Part four of the Act addresses licensing (Articles 11 to 22). Article 11 states that telecommunications operations may be conducted after obtaining a license from the Minister. The license as referred shall be granted by considering: a. simple procedure; b. transparent, fair, and non-discriminatory process; and c. short time of completion. Provisions on license for the telecommunications operations as referred to in paragraph (1) and paragraph (2) shall be stipulated in a Government Regulation.

Chapter IV addresses licensing. Article 57 provides that to obtain a business license for telecommunications operations in Indonesia, applicants must submit a written application to the Minister. In submitting the license application, the applicants shall meet the following requirements:
(a) being in the form of Indonesian juristic person in telecommunications field:
(b) having funding resources and human resources in telecommunications field.
Procedures for submission of the license application shall be stipulated in a Ministerial Decision.

The Minister will publicly announce business opportunities, specifying details such as the types, number, and locations of operations, as well as the application process, fees, and selection criteria (Article 58). Once an application is submitted, the Minister must approve or reject it within 60 working days; if no decision is made within this period, the principle license is automatically granted (Article 64). Following the approval process, a telecommunications operation license is issued only after the necessary facilities and infrastructure pass an operational worthiness test (Article 66). These licenses are granted without a time limit but are subject to evaluation every five years, with potential administrative sanctions for non-compliance (Article 67).

law: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.5 on Implementation of Risk-Based Businesss Licensing 2021
impact:
In Indonesia, Government Regulation Number 5 of 2021 (GR 5/2021) governs risk-based licensing for the telecommunications sector. It establishes a risk-based business licensing system applicable to various industries, including telecommunications.

Article 149 states that the definitions and regulatory framework for postal, telecommunications, broadcasting, and electronic transactions follow the relevant sectoral laws, including the Telecommunications Law No. 36 of 1999, the Broadcasting Law No. 32 of 2002, and the Electronic Information and Transactions Law No. 11 of 2008. The risk-based licensing system applies to telecommunications businesses, categorizing them based on their potential impact and regulatory requirements.

Article 150 states that the risk-based licensing requirements for telecommunications businesses. Low-risk businesses require only a Business Identification Number (NIB), while medium-low risk businesses must obtain an NIB and a self-declared Standard Certificate. Medium-high risk businesses need an NIB and a verified Standard Certificate, and high-risk businesses must secure an NIB, a fully verified business license, and regulatory approval before commencing operations. This classification ensures that higher-risk businesses, such as mobile network operators (MNOs), satellite providers, and telecom infrastructure developers, undergo stricter oversight.

Article 151 focuses on compliance, monitoring, and sanctions for telecommunications businesses. Operators must adhere to technical, security, and service quality standards set by the Ministry of Communications and Informatics, with periodic audits and performance reviews. Businesses must submit regular compliance reports, and violations can result in warnings, fines, license suspension, or revocation for severe infractions such as service disruptions, security breaches, or fraudulent activities. This regulatory framework ensures that telecommunications services operate efficiently, securely, and in compliance with national standards.

law: Regulation of Minister of Communications and Informatics No.5 on Telecommunications Operation 2021
impact:
Article 144 of the Regulation of the Minister of Communications and Informatics No. 5 on Telecommunications Operation (2021) focuses on the allocation of telecommunications numbering rather than the telecommunications business license itself. It specifies the conditions under which new telecommunications numbers can be allocated, including when a business applies for a new network or service license, when additional telecommunications services are introduced, or when numbers are required for public service purposes.

The application process requires submitting a copy of the business license for telecommunications network or service operations. For public service numbering, government institutions, state-owned enterprises (BUMN), or legal entities must submit proof of their establishment. Applications must be processed through the Online Single Submission (OSS) system, ensuring a standardized and transparent procedure.

Approval depends on compliance with existing regulations and the availability of numbering resources. If the request meets all criteria and resources are available, the numbering is allocated. However, if numbering resources are unavailable, the request is rejected.

law: Law No.27 on Personal Data Protection 2022
impact:
Indonesia's approach to cross-border data policies is primarily governed by the Personal Data Protection Law (PDP Law), which was enacted in 2022 and is set to be fully enforced by October 2024. The Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022 is Indonesia’s first comprehensive law dedicated specifically to personal data protection. It significantly updates and consolidates personal data governance compared to Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions (EIT Law) and Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012 (Regulation 82). The PDPA does not fully replace the EIT Law or Regulation 82, but it supersedes and updates many of their provisions related to data privacy, creating a more robust framework for data protection. 

Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), 2022 does not mandate strict localization but emphasizes secure data transfer practices.
Under Article 55, the PDPA allows cross-border data transfers but imposes conditions to ensure that the data is protected according to Indonesian standards. Transfers are allowed if the destination country has an equivalent level of data protection, or contractual safeguards are in place to protect the data.

Article 56 states that the Data Controller may transfer personal data to other Data Controllers and/or Data Processors outside the jurisdiction of the Republic of Indonesia in accordance with the provisions regulated in this law. It emphasizes that when transferring personal data, the Data Controller must ensure that the country where the receiving Data Controller and/or Data Processor is located provides an adequate level of personal data protection. If the level of protection is not adequate, the Data Controller must ensure that there are adequate and binding safeguards in place. If neither condition is met, explicit consent from the data subject must be obtained for the transfer.

Article 66 addresses requirements for data security and confidentiality, essential for sectors handling sensitive data, like banking and finance, mandating that personal data be processed securely to protect against unauthorized access. Articles 65 and 67 prohibit unauthorized collection, disclosure, or usage of personal data, establishing penalties for non-compliance, which directly affects financial service providers’ handling of customer data.

Article 74 of transitional Provisions states that existing data controllers and processors must comply with the new law within two years of its enactment (October 2024), allowing time for organizations to adjust their practices.
note: Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022, cross-border data transfers are permitted, including for financial data, as long as adequate protections and equivalency standards are maintained. Specifically, Article 55 requires that data transferred outside Indonesia must be protected to standards equivalent to those in Indonesia. Financial institutions must ensure that data recipients in other countries adhere to similar protection measures, either through contractual safeguards or by verifying that the recipient country has adequate data protection laws in place.

impact:
The conditional flow in Indonesia primarily apply to specific data - mainly tied to personal data and specific sectors handling sensitive data. Article 55 of the PDPL specifies that personal data related to Indonesian citizens must generally be stored in Indonesia, with exceptions for cross-border data transfers if the destination country ensures adequate protection or if the data subject provides consent.

Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) – Law No. 27 of 2022 The PDPL came into effect in 2024, and it sets out comprehensive rules for the protection of personal data in Indonesia. The law addresses data storage, processing, and cross-border data transfer requirements.
- Article 55 stipulates that personal data related to Indonesian citizens must generally be stored in Indonesia. Personal data cannot be transferred outside the country unless specific conditions are met, such as obtaining consent from the data subject or ensuring that the recipient country provides an adequate level of data protection.
- Article 56 outlines the conditions under which personal data can be transferred across borders. The transfer must comply with the principles of personal data protection, and the recipient country must have data protection regulations equivalent to Indonesia’s laws or, alternatively, a binding agreement to ensure compliance with Indonesia’s data protection standards.
- Article 59 outlines exemptions for Data Transfer: Personal data can be transferred outside Indonesia if it is for the performance of a contract or in situations where the transfer is needed for other legitimate purposes (such as fulfilling a legal obligation or providing a service requested by the data subject).
- Article 65 sets conditions for the processing of personal data, including the storage and retention periods, specifying that personal data must be stored in a way that is secure and protects against unauthorized access or loss.

Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 22/23/PBI/2020 that support conditional flow regimes of financial data as follows:
Article 109 (Pasal 109):
- Paragraph (1): Data related to individual customers may be transferred outside Indonesia, provided it complies with data protection laws and Bank Indonesia regulations.
- Paragraph (2): Bank Indonesia may halt cross-border data transfers if they conflict with regulations or national interests.
Article 63 (Pasal 63): Bank Indonesia may approve cross-border cooperation for payment systems, considering:
- Reciprocity.
- Risk management standards.
- Benefits to Indonesia's economy.

Financial Services Authority (OJK) Regulation No.11/POJK.03/2022
Article 35:
- Paragraph (1): Banks are required to place their data centers and disaster recovery centers within the territory of Indonesia.
- Paragraph (2): Banks may place their data centers and/or disaster recovery centers outside Indonesia, but only with prior approval from the Financial Services Authority (OJK).
- Paragraph (3): Specifies the criteria for systems that can be placed outside Indonesia, such as systems for global integrated analysis, risk management, anti-money laundering, and others.
Article 36:
- Outlines the requirements and procedures for banks to obtain approval from OJK to place data centers or disaster recovery centers outside Indonesia. This includes risk analysis, compliance with Indonesian laws, and ensuring OJK's ability to supervise.

The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No.20 of 2016 provides a legal framework for the protection of the use of personal data through electronic systems. The Government Regulation No. 40 of 2019 further clarifies the definition of personal data to be protected that include fingerprint, signature, iris (in eyes), disgraces, notes on mental or physical diseases.

Moreover, Law No. 27 establishes a general framework for the protection of personal data in Indonesia. It is closely aligned with international data privacy standards, and is largely modelled on the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. Data controllers, data processors and relevant parties that process personal data are given a two year transition period following the enactment of Law No. 27, thus up to 17 October 2024 to conform with it. Once the transition period elapses, all such parties must comply with all the provisions of Law No. 27 and any noncompliance thereto may possibly be enforced.

Indonesia enacted the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022, establishing Indonesia’s first dedicated and comprehensive data protection framework, akin to international standards like the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Key features of the PDPA include:
	1.	Clear Definition of Personal Data and Comprehensive Rights for Data Subjects:
Article 6: Grants data subjects the right to correct and update their data.
Article 8: Provides the right to request the deletion or termination of processing personal data.
Article 9: Allows withdrawal of consent for data processing.
Article 11: Allows data subjects to limit or suspend the processing of their data
	2.	Cross-Border Transfer Rules: Allows data transfers abroad under strict conditions, ensuring equivalent protection.
Article 55: Governs cross-border transfers, permitting them only if the destination country has adequate protection measures or appropriate safeguards are in place
	3.	Data Processing Obligations: Imposes duties on data controllers and processors for secure and lawful data handling.
Article 35: Requires data controllers to implement organizational and technical measures to ensure data protection.
Article 39: Mandates appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for entities processing sensitive data or conducting large-scale processing.
Articles 40–42: Specify reporting obligations in case of data breaches, ensuring accountability and transparency
	4.	Enforcement and Penalties: Provides for administrative sanctions and criminal penalties for violations.
Article 67: Imposes administrative fines for non-compliance.
Articles 66–68: Stipulate criminal penalties for unauthorized access, misuse, or other breaches of personal data 

However, the PDPA is still being operationalized and will fully come into effect in October 2024, alongside sector-specific regulations (e.g., financial and health) that augment its application. While this indicates progress, Indonesia’s data protection regime is still evolving and may face challenges in enforcement and harmonization across sectors.
note:
Prior to October 2024, Indonesia's data protection landscape was fragmented, with various sector-specific regulations. However, the enactment of the Personal Data Protection Law (UU Nomor 27 Tahun 2022), effective October 2024, provides a comprehensive legal framework for data protection in Indonesia. 

Indonesia's data protection framework was fragmented due to several laws that addressed specific sectors without providing a cohesive approach. Key laws included Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions, which offered limited data protection provisions; Law No. 23 of 1999 on Bank Indonesia, which focused on banking operations without addressing data privacy; Law No. 3 of 2011 on Fund Transfers and Law No. 7 of 2011 on Currencies, which regulated financial transactions but lacked comprehensive data protection measures. Additionally, various regulations from the Financial Services Authority (OJK) and the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology further contributed to the inconsistency, as they imposed specific requirements for sectors like banking and telecommunications without a unified legal framework for personal data protection across all sectors.

Personal Data Protection Law (UU Nomor 27 Tahun 2022) establishes a unified set of principles and rules for the processing and transfer of personal data, addressing many of the previous gaps in the legal framework.  While sector-specific regulations may still exist and apply alongside the general law, the PDP Law serves as the overarching and comprehensive framework.

law: Law No.27 on Personal Data Protection 2022
impact:
Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022 specifies obligations for data retention but does not define a universal minimum retention period. However, it outlines conditions for data retention, focusing on relevance to processing purposes and compliance with other laws. Relevant articles include:
- Article 42 (1): Data processing must end when the retention period is over, the processing purpose is achieved, or upon request by the data subject.
- Article 44 (1): Data must be deleted when the retention period expires unless otherwise required by regulations.
- Article 21 (1d): Requires data controllers to specify the retention period for personal data during consent acquisition.
These articles emphasize that data retention must be aligned with processing purposes and other sectoral regulations. Specific minimum periods are usually set by sectoral laws (e.g., financial or health).

Financial Sector: Regulations from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority (OJK) often mandate that financial institutions retain transaction and customer data for a minimum period of 5 years for anti-money laundering compliance.
Health Sector: Medical record retention is regulated under Ministry of Health provisions, often requiring a minimum period of 5 years for individual health data.
note:
Indonesia lacks a single, unified law establishing a universal minimum data retention period.  Instead, retention requirements are scattered across various regulations and sector-specific laws.  This fragmented approach creates inconsistencies and challenges for businesses and government agencies alike.  A harmonized, comprehensive legal framework is needed to clarify obligations, ensure data protection, and promote legal certainty.

The Electronic Information and Transactions Law (ITE Law) and its amendments do not specify a minimum data retention period. Instead, they delegate this responsibility to subordinate regulations.
Sector-Specific Variations: Different sectors (e.g., finance, health, e-commerce) have their own data retention requirements, often mandating a minimum of 5 years for certain data types. Government Regulation No. 80/2019, for example, specifies 10 years for financial transactions in e-commerce and 5 years for non-financial transactions. Government Regulation No. 46/2014 mandates 5 years for financial data related to financial reporting systems. Government Regulation No. 71/2019 requires electronic system operators to store logs for auditing purposes, but doesn't specify a minimum retention period. Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 20/2016 requires electronic system operators to maintain electronic records and logs for a minimum of 5 years. Government Regulation No. 46/2014, Article 21(5), mandates a minimum of 10 years for non-electronic health data and 25 years for electronic health data.

Domestic and/or foreign Electronic System Operators in Trade (PPMSE), as well as Intermediary Service Providers, are held liable for any legal consequences arising from the presence of illegal electronic information content.
However, this liability does not apply if the respective domestic and/or foreign PPMSE acts promptly to remove electronic links and/or illegal electronic information content upon acquiring actual knowledge or awareness of such content.

This provision does not apply to Intermediary Service Providers acting in the following capacities:
a.	As a mere conduit, meaning they only transmit information and: (1) Do not initiate the transmission; (2) Do not select the receiver of the transmission; and (3) Do not modify the information being transmitted.
b.	As a caching provider, meaning they temporarily store information solely for the efficiency of communications, provided that they: (1) Do not modify the stored information; (2) Comply with conditions on accessing such information; (3) Follow rules for updating information in accordance with widely accepted industry standards; (4) Do not interfere with lawful technologies widely used in the industry to obtain data on the use of such information; and (5) Act promptly to delete or disable access to stored information upon gaining actual knowledge that the original source has removed or disabled access to such information, or upon order by a court or authority.
c.	As a hosting provider, meaning they offer storage space for the placement or uploading of content, and: (1) Have no actual knowledge of illegal acts or information, and if there is a claim for damages, the provider was not aware of the illegal nature of the act or content; or (2) Upon acquiring such knowledge or awareness, the provider acts promptly to remove or disable access to the content.
d.	As a search engine, which functions as a provider, finder, or crawler of information and networks.
Additionally, intermediary service providers offering interactive computer services shall not be held liable or subject to legal claims for actions taken to restrict or remove access to content, if:
●	The action was voluntarily taken in good faith to restrict access to or availability of material that the user or provider believes falls under the category of illegal electronic content, without requiring a legal determination of its protected status; or
●	The action was taken to restrict public access, disable, or make such content inaccessible, either based on the provider’s own assessment or that of a third party.

law: Copyright Law No.28 2014
impact:
In Indonesia, the concept of safe harbor for copyright infringements is primarily addressed under the Law Number 28 of 2014 on Copyrights. However, the law itself does not explicitly use the term "safe harbor" as it is commonly understood in jurisdictions like the United States under the DMCA. Instead, the Indonesian law provides a framework that indirectly supports the concept through its provisions on intermediary liability and the responsibilities of online platforms. The relevant provisions in the Indonesian Copyright Law that relate to the responsibilities of online platforms and could be interpreted as providing a form of safe harbor include:
- Article 10 outlines the rights and obligations of copyright holders and users, which can indirectly affect how platforms manage user-generated content and copyright infringements.
- Article 43 discusses the limitations and exceptions to copyright, which may include provisions that affect how online platforms handle content.
- Article 44 provides for the protection of technological measures and rights management information, which can be relevant to how platforms manage and protect copyrighted content.
- Article 55 outlines the liability of service providers. It states that service providers are not liable for copyright infringement if they can demonstrate that they did not have knowledge of the infringing activity and acted promptly to remove or disable access to the infringing content upon receiving a notice.

Law No. 11 of 2008 on Information and Electronic Transactions (ITE Law). The ITE Law is another important piece of legislation that governs electronic transactions and online content in Indonesia. It does not explicitly offer a safe harbor for online platforms in the context of copyright infringement, but it touches on issues related to online content and its regulation.
- Article 15 discusses the liability of electronic system providers. It states that they are responsible for the operation of their systems but are not liable for user-generated content if they can prove that the infringement was due to force majeure, user error, or negligence on the part of the user.
- Article 27 (1) Prohibits the distribution of content that infringes on another’s rights, including intellectual property rights. This could apply to online platforms, but it does not specify the liability of platforms for user-uploaded infringing content.
- Article 28 elaborates on the prohibition of content that violates the law, including defamation, obscenity, or the infringement of intellectual property rights. Again, this article does not address safe harbor provisions or limitations on platform liability.
- Article 29 Imposes obligations on service providers to ensure their services do not violate laws, which might include copyright infringement, but it does not include protections or exemptions for service providers.

The Circular of the Minister of Communication and Information Technology No. 5/ 2016 provides the exemption to e-commerce providers from the liability for failures to comply with the relevant laws in the event of force majeure, errors, or negligence. E-commerce providers will only be responsible for prohibited content posted on their platform if they are unable to prove that the uploading of such content was caused by the users.

Government Regulation No.80/2019 provides a broad immunity to e-commerce service providers and intermediary service providers from the legal consequences arising from illegal third-party content. For e-commerce service providers, the regulation discharges them from any liability for illegal content found on their platforms, provided they have acted expeditiously to remove or disable access to such content after knowing of its existence (either by way of a report from a third party or finding it out themselves). To ensure that an e-commerce service provider is alerted of illegal content on its platform, the regulation requires such provider to provide terms of use/terms and conditions of the platform to its users and employing certain technology and/or feature in the platform for users to submit a report. For intermediary service providers, the regulation discharges them from any liability for illegal content provided that such providers are acting as a mere conduit. This will be evidenced by, among others, the provider's lack of control over the transmission. If an intermediary service provider provides an 'interactive computer service', such as a social media platform, they will be discharged from any liability for restricting or removing access to content if such action was carried out in good faith and based on a report that such content is illegal.

MOCI Regulation 5 now provides that private ESOs hosting user-generated content may be exempted from legal liability for prohibited content transmitted or distributed on their electronic systems as long as they have fulfilled their governance obligations, shared information on subscribers who uploaded the prohibited content for monitoring and law enforcement purposes, and taken down the prohibited content as regulated under MOCI Regulation 5. Private ESOs must ensure that their electronic systems do not (i) contain prohibited electronic information or documents and (ii) facilitate dissemination of prohibited electronic information or documents. They also must take down prohibited content within 24 hours or four hours (the latter is for urgent prohibited content, such as child pornography content, terrorism content and content that causes public unrest, which is very broad) after receiving the takedown notice. MOCI Regulation 5 classifies prohibited content into content that:
- is in violation of laws and regulations
- causes anxiety for society and disturbs public order based on the government’s assessment

Indonesia’s Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions (ITE Law) is the main regulation that governs online conduct, but it does not provide a safe harbor for online service providers when it comes to illegal activities carried out by users. The law addresses various illegal online activities, such as:
- Defamation (Article 27): Prohibits the dissemination of false information or defamation online. Criminalizes the distribution of illegal content (e.g., defamation, pornography, hate speech).
- Illegal Content Distribution (Article 27): Prohibits the distribution of pornography, gambling, or content that violates intellectual property rights.
- Article 28: Criminalizes the dissemination of false or misleading information.

New Indonesian Criminal Code (Law No. 1 of 2023) introduces changes that impact the intermediary liability landscape in Indonesia, particularly in the context of online platforms and corporations. The New Criminal Code significantly increases the accountability of intermediaries and corporations, requiring them to take proactive measures to prevent illegal activities and manage content effectively - Article 145 explicitly recognizes corporations (including online platforms) as legal subjects of criminal liability (Article 46).
- Article 2 recognizes living law (adat law) as a source of criminal law in Indonesia. Crimes can be prosecuted based on local customary laws if they are consistent with the principles of the national legal system and are codified or recognized by local regulations.
- Article 46: Corporations can be held liable if they fail to take preventive measures to avoid crimes or damages. This includes ensuring compliance with laws and implementing internal systems to prevent illegal activities.
Article 145: Establishes fine categories for corporate crimes, with the minimum fine for corporations set at IDR 200 million, unless otherwise specified by law.

- Article 264: Criminalizes the dissemination of uncertain, exaggerated, or incomplete information that causes public unrest, with penalties of up to 2 years imprisonment or fines up to IDR 50 million.
---
For other types of illegal activities (e.g., defamation, hate speech, fraud, or other criminal acts), there is no explicit safe harbor provision in Indonesian law. impact:
Minister of Communication and Information Technology Regulation No. 14 of 2017 states that to get a prepaid phone SIM card in Indonesia, a customer must register their phone prepaid SIM card with their valid national ID and family register card, or a passport for foreigners. For the Registration process using passport, the information to be registered includes at least name, passport number, citizenship, and place and date of birth.

Minister of Communication and Information Technology Regulation No. 21 of 2021 strengthens Indonesia’s SIM card registration process by requiring both prepaid and postpaid SIM cards to be registered with valid identity information (Article 3). Indonesian citizens must use their KTP, while foreign nationals must use their passport (Article 3). Mobile operators are mandated to verify the registration information by cross-checking it with the Dukcapil (for locals) or Immigration (for foreigners) databases (Article 4). The regulation introduces the use of digital IDs and biometric verification (such as facial recognition or electronic signatures) to streamline and secure the registration process (Article 5). It also reinforces data protection measures, ensuring personal data is securely handled in line with Indonesia’s Personal Data Protection Law (Article 6). To combat fraudulent registrations, operators must implement anti-fraud measures (Article 7), and non-registered SIM cards will be blocked (Article 8). These provisions work together to enhance telecommunications security, reduce fraud, and ensure that SIM cards are linked to verified identities.
note:
In recent years, there have been increasing concerns about privacy and government surveillance with the SIM registration process. Some users have raised concerns about the centralization of personal data and its potential misuse. The government has responded to these concerns by emphasizing that the registration process is crucial for security and combating digital fraud and terrorism.

Additionally, some discussions have been ongoing regarding the future of digital identification in Indonesia, particularly concerning the potential implementation of biometric data as part of the identity verification process for both SIM card registration and access to certain online services.

impact:
In 2014, Indonesia blocked video-sharing websites: Reddit and Imgur. In 2015, Indonesia blocked another video-sharing website Vimeo. In March 2020, the online subtitling service Subscene.com was reportedly blocked.

Since 2016, the government can prevent the dissemination of prohibited content through blockings. Minisry of Informatics and Communications can block content and users to prevent the dissemination of prohibited content, following requests by enforcement agencies or the public.

In January 2018, the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MCIT) launched “Cyber Drone 9,” a crawler system driven by AI tools that are designed to proactively detect content violations. It replaced the Trust+ system, which relied on a passive database. A specialized task force monitors the new system and reviews the material it flags for filtering and blocking; the blocking itself is still carried out by ISPs. Each ISP may employ its software for blocking and thus may blacklist additional sites at its discretion. This has increased the likelihood of arbitrary, inconsistent blocking, creating uncertainty for users seeking redress when content is wrongfully blocked. In July 2020, the MCIT stated that it planned to purchase more sophisticated technology to block more categories of negative content and websites.

In Indonesia, the primary laws enabling the blocking of commercial web content are ITE Law, GR 71/2019, and PM Kominfo 5/2020, with specific focus on illegal content, system registration, and public order. These laws reflect Indonesia’s aim to regulate its digital ecosystem while balancing governance with user freedoms.
note:
The legal framework in general broad powers are granted to the Indonesian government to regulate online content, including the ability to block access to websites and platforms.  However, these regulations don't single out commercial content for special treatment.  The blocking actions are typically based on broader criteria such as violations of Indonesian law (which could include aspects of commercial activity, but not exclusively), threats to public order, or non-compliance with registration requirements.

Vimeo faced significant challenges in Indonesia, where the platform was blocked due to government regulations concerning inappropriate content, including nudity and pornography. This blocking is part of Indonesia's broader internet censorship policies, which have seen various platforms restricted over the years. Users in Indonesia have reported difficulties accessing Vimeo, leading many to seek solutions such as VPNs to bypass these restrictions. However, the examples cited (PayPal and Steam) were blocked due to non-registration, not because of their commercial nature per se.  The regulations empower the government to block websites for various reasons, but the commercial aspect is not a primary or exclusive criterion. law: Law No.44 on Pornography 2008
impact:
Indonesia imposes restrictions on online advertising as stipulated in Article 4 of Law No. 44/2008 on Pornography. This article explicitly prohibits the creation, distribution, and use of pornographic content, including in advertisements across print, electronic, and online media. Consequently, online ads containing or promoting pornographic elements are classified as illegal content. Enforcement of this regulation may lead to measures such as blocking and filtering by Internet Service Providers (ISPs):
• Blocking may be applied to websites that entirely host pornographic advertisements.
• Filtering can restrict access only to specific ad content that violates the law. While internet shutdowns are not specifically mentioned in Article 4 of Law No. 44/2008, they could in principle be used as a last resort to halt access to illegal content, including pornographic ads.

The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 5 of 2020 on Private Electronic System Operators mandates both local and offshore Private Electronic System Operators (ESOs) to register their businesses to the relevant ministry through the online single submission system. Offshore ESOs should also appoint liaison officers, who have to be domiciled in Indonesia.
