This policy extends to companies offering digital services accessible to Indonesian users, regardless of their physical presence in the country. Registration entails compliance with content moderation rules, including the obligation to remove unlawful content within specified timeframes, and adherence to local data protection standards. In Indonesia, the import licensing procedures for electronics and ICT goods have undergone several updates but remain largely restrictive. Initially governed by MOT Regulation No. 56/2009 and later extended by MOT Regulation No. 83/M-DAG/PER/12/2012 (Article 6 and 9 set non-automatic import licensing procedures, including pre-shipment verification and restrictions on ports of entry), the framework required non-automatic import licenses, pre-shipment verification at importers’ expense, and restricted imports to designated ports. 

Subsequent regulations, including MOT Regulation No. 28/2020 (Article 19A introduced a list of products exempted from non-automatic import licensing procedures but continued to enforce these procedures for certain electronics, including mobile phones), replaced these earlier decrees while maintaining significant controls over ICT imports. Regulation 28/2020 simplified licensing for specific product categories by exempting certain items, yet it preserved non-automatic licensing requirements for electronics like mobile phones.

Additionally, MOT Regulation No. 36/M-DAG/PER/7/2014 (Article 9 include requirements for verification at the loading port, such as the Notification Letter or Distribution Permit Agreement Letter for certain regulated products) and its amendment (MOT Regulation No. 51/2020) mandate strict entry-point restrictions and pre-shipment verification for compliance. Though some measures, such as the need for a “Registered Importer” designation, were eased under MOT Regulation No. 87/2015, importers still face regulatory hurdles, including technical documentation and approval processes tailored to the product type and its intended use. While there have been incremental changes to reduce procedural burdens, the general structure of regulated import licensing for electronics and ICT goods remains valid. The latest updates and specific clauses can be examined in MOT Regulation No. 28/2020 and related amendments.

Foreign companies face limitations since certain certifications (Article 7, Paragraph 1(e)), like the Distributor Certificate of Registration (STP), are only available to wholly Indonesian-owned entities. Article 7(2)(b)): Importers must maintain a minimum of 25 after-sales service centers across Indonesia.

law: Regulation of the Minister of Finance Regulation No.190/PMK.04/2022 of 2022 on the Release of Imported Goods for Use 2022
coverage: Software and Digital products transmitted electronically
impact:
The Ministry of Finance Regulation No. 190/PMK.04/2022 (PMK-190), which specifically addresses the customs and VAT obligations for imported intangible goods such as software and digital products transmitted electronically. This regulation mandates that companies must submit an import notification form within 30 days of payment and pay relevant import duties and taxes, including VAT and income tax. It applies to software purchased electronically, including via downloads.

Article 34 on the Import of Intangible Goods. Intangible goods, such as software and other digital products, can be imported through electronic transmission. These goods are exempt from certain requirements, including transportation and manifest submission, unloading and storage in customs areas, and physical inspection. Customs obligations for these intangible goods are monitored through a customs audit mechanism. 
Article 35: Customs obligations for intangible goods are fulfilled using the Import Notification Form (PIB). The PIB must be submitted within 30 days from the date of payment for the intangible goods. Import duties for intangible goods are calculated according to the specified method in Article 22, which involves calculating duties based on the customs value. 
Article 36 imposes a collection of VAT and other taxes on intangible goods, conducted according to tax regulations concerning the use of intangible taxable goods from outside the customs area within the customs area.
note:
Navigating the import of digital goods into Indonesia requires understanding new customs procedures and compliance with value-added tax (VAT) obligations. In 2023, Indonesia introduced updated customs procedures for digital products, including software and other electronically transmitted goods. These products now fall under a broader classification system for customs purposes, with regulations aiming to capture a wide range of digital imports. Importers must provide clear data regarding the goods, and failure to comply can lead to delays or penalties.

One key update for digital imports is the VAT imposition on digital goods, including software. As of 2023, Indonesia has extended its VAT obligations to include digitally delivered products. This means that companies importing software and other digital goods into Indonesia must adhere to VAT compliance, which could involve submitting specific documentation and paying taxes based on the product’s value. The VAT concerns also include the challenge of determining the correct VAT rate for products sold via foreign e-commerce platforms, where taxes may be due despite international transactions.

impact:
The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MOCI) Regulation No. 12/2019, which amends MOCI Regulation No. 41/PER/M.KOMINFO/10/2009, telecommunications operators in Indonesia are required to allocate at least 50% of their capital expenditures (CapEx) for network development to locally sourced components or services. This regulation aims to promote the use of domestic products and services in the telecommunications sector. Furthermore, operators must submit an annual report detailing the percentage of local content they have procured, which must be verified by either a government agency or an accredited survey institution. These provisions are designed to encourage local industry participation in network infrastructure development.

MOCI Regulation No. 12/2019 Article 6 Specifies that components of telecommunications materials/devices with at least 50% local content are considered to have 100% local content. This effectively mandates that telecommunications operators allocate a significant portion of their capital expenditures (CapEx) for network development to locally sourced components or services. Article 10 states that Telecommunications operators are required to conduct a self-assessment of their local content achievement (TKDN) for both capital and operational expenditures annually. They must report these findings to the Director General by April 30 of the following year. Article 11 states reported local content achievements must be verified by either a government agency or an accredited survey institution. This ensures compliance and encourages the use of domestic products and services in the telecommunications sector.
timeframe: Since October 2009, last amended in October 2019

impact:
The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MOCI) Regulation No. 27/2015, repealed under the MOCI Regulation No.13/2021, continues to mandate local content requirements (LCR) for telecommunications equipment such as 4G smartphones. As of 2017, the minimum local content level was set at 40% for base stations and 30% for subscriber stations (smartphones, modems, etc.). These regulations aim to foster domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on imports in the telecommunications sector.

As of October 2024, Apple’s iPhone 16 are banned in Indonesia, it stems from the company’s failure to meet the local content threshold required for smartphones under these regulations. The LCR mandates that at least 30% of the components in devices like smartphones be sourced locally. Despite Apple’s efforts to invest locally, such as supporting developer academies, its production in Indonesia fell short of fulfilling these requirements, prompting the ban. This situation highlights Indonesia’s ongoing push to strengthen its domestic manufacturing capabilities, a central component of its regulatory framework, especially in high-tech sectors like telecommunications.

MOCI Regulation No. 27/2015 Article 4 mandates that telecommunications equipment, including base stations and subscriber stations (such as smartphones), must meet specific local content thresholds.
- Base Stations: The minimum local content level is set at 40%.
- Subscriber Stations (Smartphones, Modems, etc.): The minimum local content level is set at 30%.

impact:
Law No.20 of 2014 states that Indonesia National Standards (SNI) can be developed in accordance with the international standards by taking into account the considerations of national interest and global competition. 

The development of Indonesian National Standard (SNI) is regulated under the Regulation of the National Standardization Body Number 8 of 2022. This regulation does not stipulate that stakeholders involved in the development of SNI originate solely from within the country. However, they are required to meet the stipulated criteria.

The formulation of the Indonesian National Standard (SNI) is carried out in a transparent manner and is accessible to the public via https://sispk.bsn.go.id. The public may provide input and feedback on the Draft SNI under development during the public enquiry stage.

Law No. 20/2014 on Standardization and Conformity Assessment establishes the framework for standardization and conformity assessment. It requires that regulated products meet mandatory SNI and undergo conformity assessment. Article 5 stipulates that technical standards should prioritize “national interests,” which can implicitly limit foreign participation in the process. And Article 8 outlines the formation of technical committees (komite teknis), which are predominantly comprised of local experts, without explicit provisions for foreign stakeholders. Article 41 states that technical standards should be based on consultation, but there is no explicit mechanism for notifying foreign stakeholders or publishing drafts for review.

Government Regulation No. 34/2018 on Trade Goods Certification and Standardization which serves as an implementing regulation for the provisions outlined in Law No. 20/2014, provides detailed rules and operational guidelines for enforcing the law, particularly concerning trade goods that must meet mandatory SNI or other technical standards.
note:
Indonesia's practice may conflict with WTO TBT Agreement Article 2, which encourages members to ensure transparency and non-discriminatory participation in the preparation of technical regulations. Article 2.11 requires that members promptly publish technical regulations. Indonesia has been criticized in WTO TBT committee reviews for not consistently doing this.  According to the International Trade Administration, the development of digital and technical standards in Indonesia is often heavily influenced by the government ("the only national standards permitted are Indonesian National Standards (SNIs) and BSN is responsible for their formulation"), with limited input from the private sector. This can result in standards that may not align with international norms, creating compliance challenges for businesses, especially those with global operations.

law: ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangement for Electrical and Electronic Equipment 2002
impact:
Based on the ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangement for Electrical and Electronic Equipment, Article 3, a member state shall accept or recognize the test reports and certifications issued by the testing laboratories and certification bodies of other parties.

Electronic products that are subject to mandatory implementation of the Indonesian National Standard (SNI) are not eligible for self-certification of product safety. Compliance with SNI requirements must be demonstrated through third-party certification, and therefore, certifications cannot be conducted solely by the suppliers.

Government Regulation No. 46/2021, which replaces the Government Regulation No.52/2000 stipulates that a certificate of approval is required for IT and telecommunication equipment to be sold or imported into the Indonesian market. The certificate of approval is issued by the Directorate General of Resources and Equipment for Post and Information Technology (SDPPI). The SDPPI Kepdiejen Postel No.3/2020 allows third party-certification from Conformity Assessment Bodies (CABs) from a number of countries.

Self-certification limitations for product safety, particularly concerning radio transmissions, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), and electromagnetic interference (EMI), are governed by several regulatory frameworks under the Directorate General of Resources and Equipment Standardization for Post and Informatics (SDPPI).

- SDPPI Regulation No. 7 of 2021 establishes the Type Approval process for telecommunication and radio frequency devices. Products must undergo testing in SDPPI-accredited laboratories to ensure compliance with EMC/EMI standards such as CISPR 32 and EN 301 489. Self-certification is not permitted; all results must be verified through accredited entities.
- SDPPI Regulation No. 109/2024 strengthens mandatory EMC testing parameters, such as conducted emissions and radiated emissions, for telecommunication equipment. This regulation requires conformity assessment through independent third-party testing labs accredited by SDPPI.

Foreign manufacturers are required to appoint a local Indonesian company to manage the Type Approval application and certification process. This includes the submission of technical documents and test reports.

law: Regulation of the Minister of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia No.16 on Operational Provisions for the Certification of Telecommunication Equipment and/or Devices 2018
impact:
The Minister of Communication and Information Technology (Kominfo) Regulation No. 16/2018 on Certification of Telecommunication Tools and Equipment does not allow manufacturers to self-certify their products’ compliance with Indonesian standards. Instead, a third-party testing body must assess compliance.

- Article 2: Requires all telecommunications equipment, including devices with radio transmission and EMC/EMI implications, to be certified before they can be marketed or used in Indonesia. Certification must be obtained from designated certification bodies, accredited by Kominfo. 
- Article 4, compliance with the Technical Requirements for telecommunication tools and/or equipment as referred to in Article 2 paragraph (1) must be proven by a Certificate through the certification process. 
- Article 6: Every telecommunication tool and/or equipment manufactured, assembled, or imported for trade and/or use within the territory of the Republic of Indonesia must be certified. Telecommunication tools and/or equipment that continue to be manufactured, assembled, or imported for trade in the territory of the Republic of Indonesia after three years from the effective date of the Certificate must be re-certified by the Certificate holder. 
- Article 23: Testing centers, as referred to in Article 22, conduct testing, the results of which are in the form of a Test Report. 
- Article 22 The testing centers include: a. Domestic Testing Centers; and b. Foreign Testing Centers.
note: Indonesia has specific product screening and testing requirements across various sectors, particularly for electronics, telecommunications, and consumer goods. These requirements are enforced to ensure compliance with Indonesian technical standards (e.g., SNI – Standar Nasional Indonesia) and sector-specific regulations.

impact:
Indonesia has the SNI ISO/IEC 19790:2015 standard, which regulates information technology, security techniques, and security requirements for cryptographic modules (ISO/IEC 19790:2012, IDT). 

The National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN) is currently preparing a draft Agency Regulation concerning the Implementation of Indonesian Cryptographic Algorithms and the Cryptographic Module Security Assessment Scheme. The regulatory substance includes: general criteria and specific criteria for Indonesian cryptographic algorithms, the Indonesian cryptographic committee, and the cryptographic module security certification scheme. In this regulation, SNI ISO/IEC 19790:2015 is required to be implemented by Electronic System Operators (PSE) on Vital Information Infrastructure (IIV) protection technology.

Based on Presidential Regulation No. 47/2023 on the National Cybersecurity Strategy and Cyber Crisis Management, Indonesia emphasizes the importance of maintaining cybersecurity, including through regulations governing the use of encryption. This regulation is explicitly outlined in Article 6 of Presidential Regulation 47/2023, which addresses national cryptographic independence. Currently, Indonesia has formally adopted a national encryption policy framework that “deviates” in the sense that it emphasizes the use of domestically developed cryptographic algorithms, as stipulated in the Regulation of the National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN) No. 11 of 2024 on the Implementation of Indonesian Cryptographic Algorithms and Cryptographic Module Security Conformity Assessment. This policy can be implemented by Electronic System Operators (PSE) or Critical Information Infrastructure Operators (PIIV). 

As outlined in BSSN Regulation No. 11/2024, the reference standard used is SNI ISO/IEC 19790:2015 Information Technology — Security Techniques — Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, and the adoption of international cryptographic systems remains possible. According to BSSN Regulation No. 11/2024, there is no application of encryption standards that deviate from internationally recognized standards. Furthermore, under the Electronic Information and Transactions Law (ITE Law) and BSSN Regulation No. 11/2024, foreign encryption products are required to undergo a certification process before being used in Indonesia. 

Although there is no explicit obligation to disclose trade secrets, the certification process may require the submission of proprietary technical documentation, which can raise concerns about the protection of sensitive business information. Essentially, these regulations aim to ensure that products and services comply with adopted security standards. It can be concluded that these policies are not intended to serve as a direct barrier to digital trade, as the regulations remain aligned with international standards and do not mandate the disclosure of trade secrets during the certification process.

law:
Presidential Regulation No.10 on Investment Business Sectors 2021;

Presidential Regulation No.49 on Amendments to Presidential Regulation No.10 on Investment Business Sectors 2021
impact:
The Negative Investment List (Daftar Negatif Investasi or DNI) was historically governed by Presidential Regulation No. 44 of 2016, which outlined various business sectors where foreign ownership was restricted or prohibited. This regulation has since been replaced by the Positive Investment List under Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021, which liberalized many sectors. 

Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021 on Business Fields Open to Investment, part of the Omnibus Law (Law No. 11 of 2020 on Job Creation), sets the framework for business investment in Indonesia, including e-commerce. Article 3 and Attachment distinguishes between business activities reserved for domestic investors and those open to foreign investment. E-commerce businesses with total investment value below IDR 10 billion (excluding land and buildings) are reserved for domestic investors only. For e-commerce platforms with an investment value above IDR 10 billion, there is no restriction on foreign ownership (100% ownership is permitted).

Indonesia has made significant changes to its regulations regarding foreign equity in the e-commerce sector. The e-commerce sector in Indonesia is now open to 100% foreign ownership. Article 7 of Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021 did set a condition for foreign investment in Indonesia, stating that foreign investment is only permissible in large enterprises with an investment value exceeding IDR 10 billion, excluding land and buildings. This requirement is a general condition for foreign investors across various sectors, including e-commerce. 

Additionally, Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021 is no longer applicable due to the amendments made by Presidential Regulation No. 49 of 2021. The amendments clarify and update the regulations regarding foreign investment, containing a similar Article 7 of Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021 stating that Foreign investment can only be conducted in large enterprises with an investment value exceeding IDR 10 billion (excluding land and buildings). Again, Article 7 sets a financial threshold for foreign investments, it does not limit the percentage of foreign ownership in the e-commerce sector. 

Presidential Regulation No. 49 of 2021 
- Article 2 - All business sectors are open for investment, except for sectors that are:
(a) Closed to investment.
(b) Only to be conducted by the central government.
(1a) Open sectors include those that are commercial in nature.
- Article 6 - Business sectors with specific requirements can be undertaken by all investors, including cooperatives and SMEs, under certain conditions:
(b) Investment with restrictions on foreign ownership.
(3) Specifies that sectors with restrictions on foreign ownership include:
(a) Trade in alcoholic beverages (importers, distributors, and sub-distributors).
(b) Retail trade of alcoholic beverages.

Regulation of the Investment Coordinating Board (BKPM) No. 4 of 2021 Provides technical guidelines on implementing the provisions of Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021.
- Article 5 and Article 6 clarifies the operational requirements and investment criteria, including thresholds for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
- Article 6(2) confirms that business fields designated for MSMEs (such as e-commerce businesses with a total investment below IDR 10 billion) are closed to foreign investors.
- Article 12(1) stipulates that foreign investment in Indonesia must be in the form of a Limited Liability Company (PT PMA) and comply with equity restrictions outlined in Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021.
- Article 23 elaborates on priority sectors eligible for full foreign ownership, such as large-scale e-commerce platforms (investment > IDR 10 billion).

Article 12 of BKPM Regulation No. 4 of 2021 Reiterates the 67% foreign ownership cap for telecommunication tower companies.
note: - Article 6 (Pre-Import Inspection) mandates that certain products, including ICT goods, must undergo pre-import verification by accredited surveyor agencies like Sucofindo or Surveyor Indonesia. The verification process includes physical inspection, documentation checks, and sometimes laboratory testing to confirm compliance with Indonesian standards and regulations. ICT goods, such as electronics, telecommunication devices, and computers, are generally included in these regulated categories due to their safety and environmental concerns (e.g., electromagnetic compatibility and energy efficiency).

impact:
This measure does not impose restrictions on online sales and delivery. Director General of Tax Regulation No. PER-12/PJ/2020, the provision on the imposition of Value-Added Tax (VAT) on the sale of goods and services by foreign providers to Indonesian consumers should use the phrase "and/or" instead of "or" as previously stated. This means that VAT obligations apply if foreign service providers meet either or both of the following criteria: (1) minimum annual revenue of IDR 600 million from transactions in Indonesia, and/or (2) serving at least 12,000 Indonesian consumers annually.

In accordance with Article 4(b) of PER-12/PJ/2020, the criteria are also deemed satisfied if the volume of traffic or users accessing the service from Indonesia exceeds 12,000 (twelve thousand) within one year OR 1,000 (one thousand) within one month. The term "Indonesian consumers" in the prior statement must be aligned with this provision, where "traffic or users" (not merely completed transactions) serve as the benchmark. This includes all active visits/users from Indonesia, regardless of whether a transaction occurs.

law: Law No.7 on Currency 2011
impact:
Law No. 7 of 2011 on Currency requires that all transactions within Indonesia must use Rupiah (IDR). This applies to both cash and non-cash transactions, including payments and settlements of financial obligations.
- Article 21: This article mandates that Rupiah (IDR) must be used for all transactions within Indonesia, including cash and non-cash transactions, except for certain cross-border transactions.
- Article 23: Prohibits rejecting Rupiah for settlement of obligations within Indonesia. This establishes the primacy of Rupiah in the domestic economy.
note: Regulation 50/2020 does not explicitly mandate the use of a local bank account for all e-commerce providers, it strongly implies that e-commerce businesses must work with local payment systems and comply with Indonesian currency laws (i.e., payments should generally be made in Rupiah), the exceptions applying to international trade must not always comply with all the laws and must be navigated cautiously.

law: Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 18/40/PBI/2016 on the Implementation of Payment Systems
impact:
Indonesia’s payment security standards, especially those outlined by Bank Indonesia, are aligned with international standards, such as ISO 27001 for information security management and PCI-DSS for card payment data security.

Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 18/40/PBI/2016 on the Implementation of Payment Systems sets out the requirements for the operation and security of payment systems in Indonesia:

law: Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 on Electronic Money 2018
impact:
Regulation No. 11/12/PBI/2009 last amended by the Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 requires that any e-money issuer must be licensed by Indonesia's Central Bank. In addition, the Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 added the maximum amount of stored e-money which is IDR 2 million for unregistered e-money and IDR 10 million for registered e-money.

Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 20/6/PBI/2018 on Electronic Money regulation governs electronic payments and e-wallet services in Indonesia. E-commerce providers offering digital payment services must comply with Bank Indonesia’s requirements for electronic money issuance and usage. 
- Article 4: Stipulates that electronic money issuers must obtain a license from Bank Indonesia.
- Article 9: Specifies minimum capital requirements for non-bank e-money issuers, which are linked to the value of managed floating funds. E-money issuers managing a floating fund of IDR 1 billion or more are required to obtain a license from Bank Indonesia. This applies to both closed-loop and open-loop e-money systems. Non-bank issuers managing significant floating amounts must have a minimum paid-up capital of IDR 3 billion. If the floating funds exceed IDR 9 billion, the issuer must increase their capital to IDR 10 billion plus 3% of the total floating fund. For unregistered users, the maximum floating fund per user is capped at IDR 2 million, For registered users, the cap is IDR 10 million.

Article 82: Entities conducting e-money operations prior to the regulation’s enactment (May 4, 2018) were required to apply for a license within six months of the regulation taking effect. Foreign e-commerce businesses operating in Indonesia are generally subject to the same requirements if they act as e-money issuers or integrate payment systems and must obtain a license if they issue e-money or provide similar services within Indonesia. Articles 8 and 10 specify the capital and Ownership Restrictions. At least 51% of the shares in a non-bank e-money issuer must be owned by Indonesian individuals or entities, with a maximum of 49% foreign ownership.

Indonesian Customs Tariff Book 26/PMK.010/2022;

Regulation of the Minister of Finance Regulation No.17/PMK.010/2018 on the Second Amendment to Minister of Finance Regulation Number 6/PMK.010/2017 on the Establishment of the Goods Classification System and Imposition of Import Duty Tariffs on Imported Goods 2018
impact:
Indonesia has not officially imposed custom duties on electronic transmissions such as software, multimedia, or other digital goods. However, the country has actively participated in discussions at the World Trade Organization (WTO) about ending the global moratorium on customs duties for electronic transmissions, which has been renewed regularly since 1998.

Regulation of the Ministry of Finance No. 17/PMK.010/2018 in Indonesia aligns with the WTO moratorium on customs duties for electronic transmissions, which prohibits imposing tariffs on cross-border digital goods and services. The regulation introduces Chapter 99 in the Indonesian Customs Tariff Book, which classifies intangible goods like software and other digital products under specific HS codes. However, these goods are explicitly subject to a 0% import duty rate, meaning no customs duties are imposed on electronic transmissions. This classification is more about administrative clarity and reporting rather than imposing duties.

law: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.80 on Trading Through the Electronic System (E-commerce Law) 2019
impact:
There is no explicit mandate in Indonesian law or regulations requiring the use of a .id domain name for foreign or domestic e-commerce businesses. However, the Government Regulation No.80/2019 encourages its use as part of creating a local digital presence.

Under the Regulation No.80/2019, e-commerce law states that subject to certain thresholds, foreign business actors that actively conduct e-commerce activities with consumers in Indonesia are deemed as physically present in Indonesia and conducting fixed business activities in Indonesia. These thresholds are related to (i) number of transactions, (ii) transaction value, (iii) number of shipped packages, and/or (iv) volume of traffic or number of users. A foreign business actor that meets any of the thresholds must appoint an Indonesian representative that can act on its behalf.

The regulation includes provisions related to the use of local domain names. Specifically, Article 21 of Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019 mandates the prioritization of using Indonesia’s top-level domain name (".id") for Electronic Systems in the form of websites. It also establishes sanctions for violations of this obligation, which may include: written warnings; inclusion in the priority monitoring list; inclusion in the blacklist; temporary blocking of domestic and/or foreign PPMSE services by the relevant authorized agency; and/or revocation of business licenses. 

Article 7 specifies that foreign electronic system operators that meet certain criteria (such as transaction volume or user base) are considered to have a physical presence in Indonesia. These operators are required to appoint a local representative who can act on their behalf within the country.The specific criteria for foreign PPMSEs, as referred to in Article 18 of Minister of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023, include: (a) having conducted transactions with at least 1,000 consumers within a one-year period; (b) having delivered at least 1,000 packages to consumers within a one-year period; and/or (c) having at least 1% of domestic internet users accessing their platform within a one-year period.
note: Old text Regulation 50/2020 --> Foreign e-commerce platforms in Indonesia are required to register with the Ministry of Communication and Informatics (MOCI), use a local domain (preferably a .id domain), and establish a representative office if certain thresholds of transactions or deliveries are met. Regulation 50/2020, e-commerce businesses (including foreign entities) are encouraged to use Indonesian top-level domain names (e.g., .id). Article 18: Foreign e-commerce organizers (PPSMEs), such as online platforms or digital marketplaces, must establish a local representative office if they complete over 1,000 transactions with Indonesian consumers annually, or deliver over 1,000 packages to Indonesian consumers in one year.

law: Law No.8 on Consumer Protection 1999
impact:
Indonesia's Consumer Protection Law No. 8 is a comprehensive framework aimed at protecting consumer rights, ensuring transparency, and mandating the safety and quality of goods and services in electronic commerce. However, it does not raise specific e-commerce or distance sales issues. The Law forms the foundation of consumer protection in Indonesia.
- Article 4 enumerates consumer rights, including the right to safety, accurate information, and compensation for damages.
- Article 7 imposes obligations on businesses to provide clear, truthful information about goods/services and to guarantee their safety.
- Article 8 prohibits businesses from offering goods/services that fail to meet safety, quality, or labeling standards.

It is important to note that the Consumer Protection Law is the legal basis for the implementation of consumer protection in Indonesia, although it does not specifically regulate online consumer protection.

Law (Law) No. 19 of 2016, Amendments to Law Number 11 of 2008 concerning Information and Electronic Transactions addresses digital and electronic transactions:
- Article 9 ensures consumer protection in electronic contracts, mandating transparency and clarity in terms and conditions.
- Article 18 governs the validity of electronic contracts, emphasizing fairness and requiring accessibility to contract information by consumers.

Moreover, the mechanism for regulating electronic contracts can also be found in Chapter X of Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019.

law: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.80 on Trading Through the Electronic System (E-commerce Law) 2019
impact:
Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019 explicitly stipulates that foreign Electronic System Operators in Trade (PPMSE) that meet certain criteria are deemed to have a physical presence in Indonesia and are therefore required to appoint a representative domiciled in Indonesia:
●	The obligation to provide consumer complaint services is stipulated in Article 27. 
●	The obligation to display clear and accurate product information is regulated in Article 13.
●	Article 53 states that an electronic contract must include information on the procedure for returning goods and/or services in case of any discrepancies between what was received and what was agreed upon. However, the mechanism that is explicitly detailed pertains to the refund process, as outlined in Article 71.
●	Article 32 relates to Electronic Advertising, the provisions concerning consumer rights in Electronic System-Based Trading (PPMSE) are found in Article 26. This article requires Business Actors to protect consumer rights in accordance with the prevailing laws and regulations on consumer protection;
●	One of the key consumer rights under the Consumer Protection Law (UUPK) is the right to receive compensation, reimbursement, and/or replacement if the goods and/or services received do not match the agreement or are not delivered as promised.

In addition, PPMSE conducting business activities in the context of electronic commerce (PMSE) are obligated to comply with business licensing requirements in accordance with the prevailing laws and regulations.

Furthermore, Minister of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023 serves as a regulatory framework for the governance of PMSE, aiming to establish a healthy digital trade ecosystem and ensure consumer protection, while taking into account the ever-evolving nature of PMSE business models.

It is important to note that Regulation 31/2023 does not stand alone, but rather refers to and aligns with other relevant laws and regulations, including those governing goods distribution, electronic system operators, and others.

impact:

law:
Law on Public Procurement No.30/NA 2017;

Instruction of Implementation of Law on Public Procurement No.0477/MOF 2019
impact:
The Public Procurement Law stipulates that public procurement contracts shall consist of the principle contents, such as names of the contracting parties, purpose, price, scope, rights and obligations, perform customs, etc. (See Article 49). The scope can include software. However, no requirement to surrender patents, source codes or trade secrets, or use specific encryption in order to win tenders is found.

There is no explicit requirement for bidders to surrender patents, source codes, or trade secrets as a condition for participating in tenders. However, the Public Procurement Law (Article 15) mentions that "The information required by this Article shall be limited to the subject of the contract; the procuring entity shall protect the technical or trade secrets of the bidders disclosed during this procedure". This indicates a clear stance on maintaining the confidentiality of sensitive bidder information, without requiring disclosure beyond what is necessary for the evaluation. There is no specific mention of encryption requirements in any of the tender-related documents.

law:

Instruction of Implementation of Law on Public Procurement No.0477/MOF 2019
impact:
The Public Procurement Law explicitly states that contractors, suppliers or consultants meeting all conditions shall be given domestic preference and considered to be awarded the contracts. Conditions for domestic preference are set out in separate regulations (Article 45 domestic preference). The domestic preference shall apply for international competitive bidding only. 

According to the Instruction of Implementation of Law on Public Procurement No.0477/MOF (Clause 14):
1. For works and maintenance: If a local bidder's bid price is not exceed 7.5% of an international bidder's bid price, the local bidder will be considered as the winning bidder for works. 
2. Supply of goods: Preference is given to goods manufactured in Lao PDR to promote domestically manufactured goods. Bidding documents shall clearly indicate any preference to be granted to domestically manufactured goods indicating production-base (origin) and the information required to establish the eligibility of a bid for such preference. The nationality of the manufacturer or supplier is not a condition for such eligibility.

impact:
Under the Investment Promotion Act, both domestic and foreign investors have the right to invest in all investment sectors and areas which are not prohibited by the law of the Lao PDR (Articles 67.1 and 3). The Act introduces a controlled business list, including businesses that are sensitive to national security, public order, national fine tradition, and socio-environmental impact. There is no foreign investment ownership restrictions in sectors relevant to the digital trade. 

Moreover, Law on Investment Promotion Article 4 (Government policies on investment promotion), the Government promotes investment in all sectors, business operations and in areas throughout the country except for the areas and business operations which are detrimental to national security, natural environment, at present and in long-term, public health and fine national cultures. Article 40 (Term of Investment for general investment), investment in general investments has no term limit except for those activities of which term limits have been specified by regulations of relevant sector authority.
note:
1.Lao PDR has taken steps towards improvement of its investment climate. The relevant legal framework was streamlined through amendment of the Law on Investment Promotion, which has reflected numbers of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) recommendations and is aligned with the ASEAN Comprehensive Investment Agreement (ACIA).

2.Main regulations governing FDI in Lao: the Law on Enterprise No. 46/NA, dated 26 December 2013 (the Law on Enterprise) and the Law on Investment Promotion No. 14/NA, dated 17 November 2016 (the Law on Investment Promotion).

3. The general rule is that a 100 per cent foreign-owned investment is accepted under Lao law. There are no restrictions on foreign investment in Laos, except as otherwise specifed. The Law on Enterprise No. 33/NA, dated 29 December 2022 (the Law on Enterprise) and the Law on Investment Promotion No. 14/NA, dated 17 November 2016 (the Law on Investment Promotion), does not set out general prohibitions for foreigners that prevent them from holding 100 per cent of the share equity in a company in Laos. However, there are specific regulations that apply to specific industries (ICT not part of the list), and that impose stipulations on foreign investors, such as a requirement to partner with a Lao national. Some of these activities are listed in the Notifcation of the List of Business Activities for Foreign Investors No.1327/MOIC. For sectors like software development, e-commerce, and ICT services, the notification does not provide specific details, but generally, full ownership is allowed unless other regulations are applied.

4. Article 41 (Amended) (Concession investments), concession investment is an investment for which an investor is authorized by the Government in accordance with relevant laws and regulations to develop and operate a business notably concession of land, development of special economic zones, zones for industrial processing for export, mining, electric energy development, aviation and telecommunication. Therefore, foreign investors cannot own land but can only lease it, which is a national treatment. This is of significance for the telecom sector e.g. land requirement for the contraction of a datacenter or software development research parks (Possibly a new sub-pillar under the Telecom sector pillar 5).

law: Law on Investment Promotion Act No.14/NA 2010
impact:
The Law on Investment Promotion introduces a national security screening. Article 4 states that foreigners may invest in any sector or business except those that the government deems to be detrimental to national security, health, or national traditions, or to harm the natural environment at present and in long-term, public health and fine national cultures. impact:

law: Law on Investment Promotion Act No.14/NA 2010
impact:
According to the Law on Investment Promotion Act Article 41 (Amended) (Concession investments),  concession investment is an investment for which an investor is authorized by the Government in accordance with relevant laws and regulations to develop and operate a business notably concession of land, development of special economic zones, zones for industrial processing for export, mining, electric energy development, aviation and telecommunication. Therefore, foreign investors cannot own land but can only lease it, which is a national treatment. Additionally, ISIC 6110, 6120 and 6130 are related to telecomminucation services. These sectors have to receive an investment license prior, thus a screening requirement for this sector.

Article 2 and Article 3 of the Decree describe the screening mechanisms for investments in Lao PDR. Investments in sectors listed as controlled, which impact national security, social stability, and the environment, require screening and approval by relevant agencies, facilitated by a one-stop service unit that collaborates with the committee for promotion and management of investment. For concession investments, such as land concessions and the development of special economic zones, the approval process is extended, with screening taking up to 65 working days. These mechanisms aim to ensure that investments align with national priorities, excluding those that threaten stability, security, or the environment. While the government promotes investment across various sectors, businesses that could negatively impact national stability or violate other regulations are excluded from this promotion.

The Telecommunications Law does not explicitly ban or impose direct foreign equity limits for telecommunications businesses (nor in the FDI as discussed in the FDI Pillar). Article 4 of the Telecommunications Law encourages domestic and foreign individuals or entities to invest in the telecommunications sector, indicating that foreign investments are allowed under the licensing system guidelines. Foreign entities must adhere to investment and enterprise operations laws, including the requirement to apply for a telecommunications business license.

law: Law on Intellectual Property Right No. 50/NA 2023
impact:
Since January 2024, the Law on Intellectual Property Right No.50/NA replaces the Law on Intellectual Property No. 38/NA, dated 15 November 2017 (Article 141 Implementation). 

Article 6 (The Scope of Application of the Law) provides that this law is applicable to domestic and foreign individuals, legal entities and organizations who are implementing and involving in intellectual property activities in the Lao PDR.

Moreover, Article 27 (revised) (Filing of Applications) states that domestic or foreign individuals, legal entities or organizations may apply for registration of their industrial property with the Minsitry of Industry and Commerce or with an international intellectual property registration organization to which the Lao PDR is a party. Any individual, legal entity or organization residing in a foreign country wishing to apply for industrial property registration shall have a business premise or an authorized representative in the Lao PDR. The applicant without a business premise or residence in the Lao PDR shall appoint an authorized representative in the Lao PDR to carry out transactions related to intellectual property in the Lao PDR.

law: Law on Intellectual Property Right No. 50/NA 2023
impact:
Since January 2024, the Law on Intellectual Property Right No.50/NA replaces the Law on Intellectual Property No. 38/NA, dated 15 November 2017 (Article 141 Implementation). 

Under Chapter 4 Rights and obligations of Industrial Property Rights Owner, Article 47(5) (Rights of the Industrial Property Right Owner), and Article 56 (Term of Protection of Patents) grant the Patent owners the right to file lawsuits for patent infringement, seek damages, and prevent unauthorized use of their patents. They may take legal action to protect their rights and request compensation for violations.

Article 84 (revised) (Provisional Protection) grants Provisional Protection during the period between the publication of the application for the grant of a breeder’s right and the grant of that right. These measures aim to prevent further harm while grant rights are ongoing. Additionally, Article 137 (revised) (Inspection of Intellectual Property at Border Checkpoints) stipulates that In order to intercept intellectual property violations, customs officers assigned to border checkpoints have the rights by ex-officio to inspect exported and imported goods, seize and impound goods which violate trademark, copyright and related right of the law.
note:
This information is based on the 2017 Act --> Lao PDR's Law on Intellectual Property empowers patent owners with civil and administrative procedures for enforcing their rights. They have the right to initiate lawsuits for infringement, seek damages, and prevent unauthorized use of their patents through legal action, as outlined in Articles 47 and 56. They may also request compensation for any rights violations, putting them in control of their intellectual property.

On the administrative side, the process of terminating or invalidating patents is fair and transparent. If the owner fails to maintain or renew them or if the patent does not meet the required protection standards, as provided in Articles 44 and 45, the termination is justified. Additionally, third parties are permitted to request the cancellation of improperly granted patents within five years of registration, ensuring the security of the patent system.

Provisional measures are covered under Article 74, which allows courts to grant injunctive relief to stop ongoing infringement or seize goods suspected of infringing a patent. These measures help prevent further harm while legal proceedings are underway, ensuring the effective enforcement of patent rights.

law: Law on Intellectual Property Right No. 50/NA 2023
impact:
Since January 2024, the Law on Intellectual Property Right No.50/NA replaces the Law on Intellectual Property No. 38/NA, dated 15 November 2017 (Article 141 Implementation). 

There is no restriction on patent enforcement. The law protect a patent owner for both a product or a process to prevent other from exploit the right and against infringement (Article 56 revised regarding term of protection of patents).

Article 64 (Authorization to Exploit without Permission of Patent or Petty Patent Owner): In cases of national emergency, public health crises, or critical public interest (e.g., defense or food security), the government can authorize the exploitation of a patent without the owner's permission. This applies across sectors and circumstances, allowing wide-reaching use of patented inventions to serve public needs. Such a measure could affect various industries, especially during crises like epidemics, where multiple patents related to pharmaceuticals might be impacted. Under this article, it is important to note that compensation is possible and is fair ("right holder shall have the right to propose terms for compensation, how it shall be determined, and terms for payment thereof").

law: Law on Intellectual Property Right No. 50/NA 2023
note:
Lao PDR has acceded to the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literacy and Artistic Works since December 2011.
https://www.wipo.int/treaties/en/notifications/berne/treaty_berne_255.html  

Lao PDR's copyright framework includes certain exceptions, but it lacks comprehensive provisions commonly found in other jurisdictions to balance the rights of copyright holders with the public interest (does not provide a level of flexibility, nor does it set out a comprehensive test or framework to balance the rights of the copyright owner with public interest, such as the fair dealing provisions used in countries like the UK or Canada, which allow limited use for specific purposes like research, education, or private study.). The "fair use" doctrine, which typically allows the limited use of copyrighted works without permission for purposes such as criticism, news reporting, research, or education, is not explicitly covered extensively. Although Article 115 outlines some exceptions, such as quoting works or use in teaching, these are underdeveloped compared to international standards. The framework also does not sufficiently address modern digital rights issues (translating for visually impaired persons, and limited reproduction for personal or backup use), including online infringement, digital rights management (DRM), or temporary reproductions. Additionally, there is limited guidance on how institutions like libraries and archives can use copyrighted works for preservation or public access, making these areas potential gaps in the law.

law:
Law on Intellectual Property Right No. 50/NA 2023;

Penal Code No. 26/NA 2017
impact:
Under the Act, Article 123 (revised Copyright Piracy), 'copyright piracy' refers to a copy of a work of authorship or object of related rights where a copy is made without the consent of the right holder or person duly authorized by the right holder in the country of production, shall be a violation of this law. 

Chapter 4 of the Intellectual Property Right Act introduces rights of the copyright owners. Article 102 prescribes that no individual, legal entity or organization other than the author shall undertake any of the acts described in Article 100 (moral rights), such as the rights to make a collection of such works, reproduce such work, or tranlsation of such works.

Moreover, the Penal Code regulates the criminal charges for infringers and the punishments and fines relating to IP infringement (fines and punishment are mainly related to cybercrime offense such as pornographic content dissemination or financial identity theft). 

The following apply broadly to all forms of intellectual property rights, including not only patents but also copyrights and potentially other types of IP rights. Articles 47(5) and 56 grant all IP rights holders, including patent and copyright owners, the ability to file lawsuits for infringement, seek damages, and prevent unauthorized use of their rights. Legal action can be pursued to protect their IP and request compensation for any violations. Articles 44 and 45 allow administrative actions to terminate or invalidate any IP rights, including patents and copyrights, in cases where the rights are not properly maintained or do not meet required standards, and also allow third parties to request the cancellation of improperly granted IP rights. Article 84 provides provisional protection for all IP rights, including copyrights, during the application process, preventing harm before the rights are fully granted. Additionally, Article 144 allows individuals or entities to file complaints for provisional measures to prevent IP infringement, prevent goods from entering commerce, and preserve evidence of alleged infringements, which includes measures for copyright protection.
note:
Lao PDR faces several online copyright enforcement issues due to the lack of a detailed framework for dealing with digital rights management (distribution of digital works online, such as music, films, or e-books), online piracy (online infringement through streaming platforms, torrent sites, or file-sharing services), and the responsibilities of internet service providers. The absence of clear takedown procedures, safe harbor provisions, and cross-border enforcement mechanisms makes it difficult to effectively protect copyright in the digital environment. (probably going to the pillar related to safe harbor or digital content) 
Secondary source: https://www.tilleke.com/insights/intellectual-property-rights-enforcement-laos/

According to the USTR 2023, despite the presence of counterfied goods in marketplaces, Lao PDR continues to improve IP regime and increase public awareness. With the United States Government assistance, Lao PDR effectively establishes system for civil and criminal enforcement of intellectual property. https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/2023-03/2023%20NTE%20Report.pdf

Moreover, Article 126 of the Penal Code defines intellectual property violations broadly, but there is no detailed framework for digital copyright violations or specific provisions targeting the complexities of online enforcement. Article 168 Damage through Online Media and Article 171 Falsifying Computer Data interpretation might provide a temporary interpretation avenue to this regulatory gap.

law: Law on Intellectual Property Right No. 50/NA 2023
impact:
The Law on Intellectual Property Rights Article 20 (Trade Secrets) provides that a trade secret is a secret information which cannot be disclosed regarding to formula, production process or any information which has commercial value in the sense
that it is not known among or readily accessible to persons within the circles that normally deal with the kind of information in question.

Article 61 (Rights of Proprietor of Trade Secret) states that the proprietor has the right to prevent the unauthorized disclosure, acquisition, or use of the trade secret by others without consent, provided such actions are contrary to honest commercial practices. However, exceptions apply, such as when the information is obtained through reverse engineering, laboratory testing, or other lawful means without a confidentiality obligation. The proprietor also has the right to take legal action and claim compensation for damages resulting from infringements, as well as to prevent individuals, legal entities, or organizations from misappropriating the trade secret. Additionally, the proprietor may disclose, withdraw, utilize, or transfer the trade secret to others, setting conditions for maintaining confidentiality. Finally, the proprietor can enforce confidentiality obligations on individuals lawfully in control of the trade secret, with such obligations continuing beyond the termination of employment or contractual relationships, as long as the information remains confidential.

Note that the exceptions are the legitimate means by which third parties may lawfully obtain or use trade secret information without it being considered a violation of trade secret rights. These exceptions are not about mandatory disclosure of trade secrets.
note: Article 62 (Protection of Test or Other Data) addresses data exclusivity. Undisclosed test or other data submitted for marketing approval of pharmaceutical or agricultural chemical products containing a new chemical entity is protected for five years from unfair commercial use and disclosure without the originator’s consent. Others may not rely on this data for product approval during that period without permission. Violations are deemed acts of unfair competition, and data owners have the right to take legal action.

Decision on the Management of Telecommunications and ICT No.3583/MoTC 2022
impact:
Service providers shall collectively share the telecommunication infrastructure without discrimination in terms of conditions, quality and services based on mutual benefit to avoid overlapping investment and promote efficient use of resources. This principle encourages fair access to infrastructure among providers​ (Article 20 Utilization of Infrastructure). The telecommunication infrastructure means buildings and structures, including equipment and transmission line to support the telecommunication network services, such as: duct, pole, mast, tower, antenna, optic fiber, copper wire, mixture wire, transformers (Article 15 Telecommunication Infrastructure). 

In the Decision on the Management of Telecommunications and ICT No. 3583 (2022), it emphasizes that telecommunications providers are required to share essential infrastructure, such as radio towers and core network elements, to ensure efficient use of resources and to avoid unnecessary duplication. This decision further clarifies obligations related to sharing infrastructure for various telecommunications networks, including satellite and terrestrial networks​.

Foreigners are permitted to invest in telecommunication business.

There are four authorized enterprises (LTC, ETL, UNITEL, and TPLUS) providing fixed and mobile telecommunications services in Lao PDR, and the fifth (Sky Telecom) holds a mobile license but currently only offers internet access. All of them have some share of government ownership.

impact:

law: Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA 2017
impact:
The Law on Electronic Data Protection specifies that the delivery or transfer of data must be performed as follows:
- with the consent of the data subject and guarantee that the transferee can protect such data;
- with the encryption of important information, such as financial, accounting, and investment data and with the electronic certificate issued by the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunication (Article 25);
- without forging the source of data sent or transferred;
- that the transfer must be in accordance with the agreement of the transferee and transferor; and
- that the transfer must be stopped upon refusal by transferee.

 The scope of the Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017) primarily covers the protection of personal data and other sensitive data. Specifically, Article 2 (Definitions) and Article 4 (Scope of Application) provide insights into the applicability:
- Article 2 defines personal data as any information relating to an individual, which can be used directly or indirectly to identify that person.
-Article 4 clarifies that the law applies to personal data and the management, processing, and storage of such data by both public and private sector entities within Lao PDR. This includes ensuring appropriate levels of security and confidentiality for handling personal data. The law, therefore, explicitly focuses on the protection of personal data and outlines measures for safeguarding the privacy of individuals, without extending to all categories of non-personal or generic data.
- Article 10: Defines sensitive data as information that cannot be accessed, used, or disclosed without the consent of the Information Owner. This includes information on financials, health, personal data, etc.
-Article 11: Outlines the responsibilities of the Data Administrator, including ensuring that sensitive data is adequately protected.
-Article 15: Requires periodic risk assessments, backup systems, and other measures to safeguard sensitive data. Specifies requirements for protecting sensitive data, including ensuring secure storage and conducting annual risk assessments.
- Article 16: Addresses encryption requirements for transferring sensitive data, specifically mentioning that important documents (e.g., financial, banking, and investment data) must be encrypted during cross-border transfers.

The transfer of private data outside of Lao PDR is subject to the express consent of data subject and compliance with law (Article 17 Sending or Transferring of Electronic Data).

law: Decree on the Financial Consumer Protection No. 225/GOL 2020
impact:
There is no specific mention in the documents regarding conditional flow regimes for all sectors. However, there are provisions and requirements for specific types of data, mainly sensitive data and financial data, that must be handled with extra security measures. Sensitive data (e.g., financial, medical, customer information) must be handled with explicit consent from the data owner and must be encrypted when being transferred, especially across borders. Additionally, the Decree on Consumer Protection Concerning Financial Services, which ensures that financial institutions must protect customer data and may not transfer sensitive financial information without proper safeguards.
- Article 21: Ensures that financial institutions take responsibility for collecting and handling customer information with transparency, including obtaining consent.
- Article 30: Discusses provisions to protect sensitive financial information and customer data, ensuring financial institutions implement proper safeguards for transferring data.

Lao PDR does not have comprehensive data protection law. The data protection in Lao PDR mainly refers to the protection of data in electronic format. The protection can be found in specific regulations, such as the Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA, Law on Prevention and Combating Cybercrime No. 61/NA, and Penal Code No. 26/NA. 

Specifically, under the Electronic Data Protection No. 25/NA, the electronic data refers to general data (data of individual, legal entities or organizations) and specific data (official/personal data that not allow individual, legal entities or organizations to access, use or disclose without permission from the owner or relevant organizations) (Articles 8-10). Additionally, in August 2018, to clarify the requirements under the Law on Electronic Data Protection, the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications issued the Guidelines on the Implementation of the Law on Electronic Data Protection No. 2126/MoPTC. The E-Data Protection Guidelines provide greater clarity on the classification of electronic data, the compliance obligations of data managers, and rules associated with regulated data protection activities. These Guidelines cover: (i) data collection; (ii) electronic data inspection; (iii) saving/storing of electronic data; (iv) maintaining electronic data; (v) using and disseminating electronic data; (vi) transmission and transfer of electronic data; (vii) access to electronic data; (viii) amending and updating electronic data; and (ix) deletion of electronic data.

Lao PDR has no comprehensive data protection framework that applies universally across all sectors. Instead, the country has adopted a more sector-specific (sectoral) approach to data protection. The Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017) does provide guidelines for the handling and processing of sensitive data, such as personal, financial, and medical information, but these rules are often integrated into other sectoral regulations. Lao PDR is still in the process of developing a more robust data protection regime, with ongoing efforts to enhance the legal and institutional framework for data security​ (ESCAP-2022-PB-Readiness)​ (Implementation Guide). However, the country has not yet enacted a comprehensive, cross-sectoral data protection law similar to the GDPR or California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), which would apply universally across all sectors.

4. Based on the main laws and regulations above, it is difficult to anticipate the category of data cookies and location data according to the ambiguous definitions of general data, sensitive data, and personal data. (https://www.dlapiperdataprotection.com/index.html?t=law&c=LA) 


No references to anonymized or de-identified data appear explicitly in the current data protection laws of Laos. The Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017) does not specifically define or discuss the treatment of anonymized or de-identified data. The focus of the law is more on the protection of personal data and sensitive data, which includes financial, medical, and other types of personal information, but there is no explicit guidance on how anonymized or de-identified data should be handled or whether it is exempt from protection measures. Without a legal provision for anonymization, data controllers in Laos are still required to follow existing protections, including obtaining consent for processing and transferring data, even if that data has been anonymized in practice.

- Data Subject Rights (Right to be Informed, Right of Access, Right to Rectification, Right to Restriction of Processing, Right to Data Portability, Right to Object, Right to erasure "right to be forgotten").

impact: There are no explicit minimum data retention periods mentioned in the Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017). law: Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime No.61/NA 2015
impact: Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime No. 61/NA (2015) specifies that service providers must retain computer traffic data for a minimum period. According to Article 40 (Prohibitions for Service Providers) of the law, service providers are prohibited from deleting computer traffic data for a minimum of 90 days if they have a connection system, and 365 days if they do not. law:
Standard Law (Amended) No.49/NA 2014;

Decree on the Implementation of the Law on Standardization No.234 2012
impact:
Lao Standards is the standards that is adopted by the National Standard Council and promulgated by the Ministry of Science and Technology. Lao Standards, the abbreviation in Lao is “mor lor” and in English is “Lao Standard or “LS” (Article 16 Lao Standards). 

The development of Lao Standards shall comply with the following principles to ensure the conformity with the foreign, regional and international standards (Article 17 Principles for Developing Lao Standards). The use of technical terms for the establishment of standards shall ensure consistent with the terminologies used by the International Standard Organization (ISO) (Article 15 Use of Technical Terms). 

Moreover, individual, legal entity, or organization and the National Standard Council wishing to develop Lao Standard shall submit a proposal to the Ministry of Science and Technology (Article 20 Procedures for Developing Lao Standards). Lao PDR became a signatory to the ASEAN Consultative Committee on Standards and Quality (ACCSQ), ISO, and the International Electrotechnical Commission Asia-Pacific Regional Centre (IEC-APRC). The ISO/IEC Guides 21-1 and 21-2:2005 are adopted.

The Standard Law (Amended) No. 49 encourages international cooperation and explicitly states that the Lao government promotes the involvement of both the domestic and foreign private sectors in standardization activities​. Article 4 (Policy on Standardization) specifically encourages foreign entities to participate in standardization activities, including development, implementation, and management of standards​. This includes participation in the development and implementation of standards, as well as management and inspection, suggesting that there is no formal restriction on foreigners or foreign entities from being involved in the process. 

Additionally, the Decree on the Implementation of the Law on Standardization No. 234 (2012): Article 3 (Participation between Public and Private Sectors): This article encourages the private sector, including foreign entities, to participate in the development of standards and conformity assessment procedures​.

Lao PDR has specific technical standards for ICT goods, impacting several product categories under relevant HS codes. These standards, which may differ from international benchmarks, favor products that can easily align with local regulatory requirements. According to Article 8 of the Decision on the Inspection and Certification of ICT Equipment No. 2118/MPT (2018), all imported ICT equipment, including products under HS Code 8517 (telecommunication equipment, e.g., mobile phones, routers) and HS Code 8525 (transmission apparatus), must comply with local standards related to RF, EMC, EMF, SAR, connection, and electrical safety. Article 12 further specifies these technical requirements.

ICT equipment, including telecommunication devices and mobile phones, must meet technical standards set by the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPT). This compliance acts as an indirect local content requirement by ensuring that devices align with national regulations, particularly in areas like radio frequency usage, electromagnetic compatibility, and network connectivity​. There is no strict local content requirement (LCR) in Lao PDR’s ICT regulatory framework. However, the country imposes strict regulatory and compliance standards for imported ICT goods, which may favor products that can easily align with local regulatory and technical standards.

According to the Decree on the Implementation of the Law on Standardization No. 234, the standards in Laos should be developed in a transparent manner, following international guidelines, such as the World Trade Organization's Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) Agreement​ (Decree on the Implementation). Foreigners or foreign entities are not explicitly barred from participating in technical committees, as the law permits cooperation with foreign experts when needed, especially for drafting standards​. However, transparency in the standard-setting process is ensured through public posting of draft standards for a period of at least 60 days (Article 5 of Procedures for the Preparation, Adoption, and Application of National Standards: This article specifies that during the drafting process, national standards must be posted on the Ministry of Science and Technology’s website for public comments for at least 60 days, ensuring transparency​), during which public comments are invited. In cases where foreign experts are involved, it suggests openness to external technical input, though there may be practical restrictions depending on the sector or context.

coverage: Horizontal, including electrical appliances and accessories
impact:
There is no explicit provision banning SDoC (Suppliers' Declaration of Conformity) entirely, but Lao PDR regulations emphasize third-party certification for certain products. Specifically, Article 50 (Voluntary Conformity Assessments) of the Standard Law (Amended) outlines that conformity assessment for technical regulations (e.g., products affecting safety) should be conducted by government conformity assessment bodies or accredited third-party entities. This suggests that SDoC might not be sufficient for some regulated product categories​.

According to Article 12 and Article 54, Lao PDR conforms to international standards for third-party certification and accepts conformity assessments from recognized bodies in countries with Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs). This implies that while SDoC is not universally permitted, third-party certifications from certain accredited bodies abroad are accepted.

Article 49 (Self-Conformity Assessment) of the Standard Law permits self-conformity assessment (SDoC) by suppliers or manufacturers, indicating that foreign businesses could use SDoC if the products are not subject to compulsory third-party conformity​. However, for high-risk products such as those involving safety concerns (e.g., EMC/EMI), third-party certification would likely be required. Thus, for some product safety related ICT  (e.g., radio transmissions, EMC/EMI): SDoC is generally not allowed, and third-party certification is preferred, especially if covered under an MRA​.

Specifically, ASEAN Framework Agreement on Mutual Recognition Arrangements provides the principles for developing sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangements (MRAs) among ASEAN member states, for instance the ASEAN Sectoral MRA for Electrical and Electronic Equipment (ASEAN EE MRA) 2002. A member state shall accept or recognize the test reports and certifications issued by the testing laboratories and certification bodies of other parties (ASEAN EE MRA Article 3). 

In addition, Article 10 of the Decision on the Management of Telecommunications and ICT No. 3583/MoTC (2022) mandates that equipment under HS Code 8517 and HS Code 8526 (radar apparatus, radio communication equipment) be tested locally to ensure compliance with domestic standards. Article 22 requires the use of certification labels to indicate compliance. These regulations create a framework that can serve as an indirect local content requirement by imposing barriers on non-compliant products, including higher compliance costs and delayed market entry for products that don't meet local standards.

impact:
Article 8 (Types of Lao Standards) of the Standard Law (Amended) lists categories of products subject to Lao standards, including products, goods, services, and environmental standards​. ICT products that involve radio transmissions or electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) could fall under these categories if they relate to safety or environmental concerns. Article 45 (Standard and Technical Regulation Conformity) mentions that products linked to safety, public health, and environmental protection must comply with standards and technical regulations​. This could include ICT products, especially those with radio transmission and EMC/EMI considerations.  Article 25 (Contents of Technical Regulations) of the Standard Law indicates that products falling under technical regulations would require testing and certification, and ICT products likely require compliance with performance and safety standards​). 

Article 46 (Principles of Conformity Assessment) stipulates that Lao PDR allows for self-assessments of conformity, including testing and inspection (for more information about the scope, see Article 5). Testing centers and laboratories shall be accredited or recognized by both domestic and foreign concerned accredited body (Article 68 Testing Centers, Laboratories). Specifically, Article 65 (Accreditation) of the Standard Law (Amended) mandates that testing centers and laboratories must be accredited and recognized by both domestic and foreign accredited bodies. The preparation, adoption and application of conformity assessment procedures shall be applied at least equally between the imported products and domestic products and between products originating in any other country (Article 53.1). 

Moreover, National Accreditation Bureau (LNAB) is a body that is officially recognized the capacity of individuals, legal entities or organizations in performing testing activities and certification of quality. The LNAB provides accreditation services for the accreditation of laboratories, certification and inspection bodies in accordance with the appropriate international ISO/IEC standards and guidance documents issued by the International Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation (ILAC) and the International Accreditation Forum (IAF) (for more information, see Article 67  Rights and Duties of the National Accreditation Bureau). Also, testing centers [and] laboratories shall be accredited or recognized by both domestic and foreign concerned accredited body (Article 68 Testing Centers, Laboratories). 

There is no blanket exemption from testing requirements. All products within the scope of technical regulations or standards in Lao PDR must undergo some form of conformity assessment. Lao PDR has clear measures in place for product testing, with acceptance of third-party results for certain products via MRAs. However, products under national technical regulations must comply with testing requirements through accredited bodies.
